findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q2
findings.headline: The Severn Valley Water Management Scheme strategy is due to go to Cabinet in December 2026, ahead of consultation, as the basis for a future major infrastructure programme.
findings.detail: The paper says the strategy is being developed with partners by March 2027. It will be the foundation for future outline business cases for a major infrastructure programme to manage water and reduce risk.
findings.matters: A potential major infrastructure programme with no business case yet is a capital commitment that finance directors and lenders would track as it firms up.
findings.figures: Cabinet in December 2026; strategy by March 2027
findings.quote: This will provide the foundation for future outline business cases for a major infrastructure programme

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q2
findings.headline: Recycling rates show a 'continued, but slow, decline', which the paper links to green-waste charging introduced in Autumn 2024.
findings.detail: The paper says green-waste subscriptions increased in 2025 compared with 2024 and hopes that will continue into 2026. It gives no recycling percentage in this report.
findings.matters: The paper ties a service decline to a charging decision, which is a trade-off between income and service performance that other councils weighing similar charges would compare.
findings.figures: Green-waste charging introduced in Autumn 2024
findings.quote: continued, but slow, decline in recycling rates continuing the impact of green-waste charging introduced in Autumn 2024

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q2
findings.headline: The Adult Social Care Transformation Programme is attributed to 'rising demand, an ageing population and ongoing support needs'.
findings.detail: The paper says the programme aligns with a new Adult Social Care Strategy and a focus on achieving the best outcomes within available resources. Early delivery is underway through the optimal care and community independence pathway.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand is one of the largest cost pressures for councils, so the council's stated reasons for a transformation programme are comparable across the sector.
findings.quote: rising demand, an ageing population and ongoing support needs have informed the Adult Social Care Transformation Programme

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q2
findings.headline: The Improvement Plan is being revised to bring together findings from external audit and assurance reports, with the refreshed plan due at Full Council in December 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the refresh draws on the Improvement Board's feedback and other activity. It states that the revised plan will be considered by Full Council in December, and sets the framework and priorities for the coming years.
findings.matters: External audit findings feeding a council-wide improvement plan show how a council is responding to audit weaknesses, which peers and lenders track.
findings.figures: Full Council in December 2026
findings.quote: bringing together findings from external audit and assurance reports, feedback from the Improvement Board and other activity

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q2
findings.headline: Corporate governance and compliance are among the main areas the paper says 'continue to be challenging'.
findings.detail: The paper says work has progressed on each of these areas during the quarter. It also says the refreshed Improvement Plan will be completed in Quarter 3 with more effective programme, performance and risk management approaches.
findings.matters: A council reporting its own governance and compliance areas as still challenging is information that auditors, lenders and peer finance officers would weigh.
findings.quote: The main areas requiring sustained attention (including corporate governance and compliance) continue to be challenging

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q2
findings.headline: A new business and budget planning approach began rolling out in Quarter 2, ahead of the February 2027 Council budget meeting.
findings.detail: The paper describes the approach as supporting a more inclusive, disciplined and transparent budget-setting process. It says the refreshed Medium-Term Financial Strategy remains on track.
findings.matters: A change to how the budget is built, ahead of the February 2027 setting, is a process change that finance officers at other councils would compare against their own.
findings.figures: February 2027 Council budget meeting
findings.quote: Roll out of the new business and budget planning approach commenced to support a more inclusive, disciplined and transparent budget-setting process ahead of Council in February 2027

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q2
findings.headline: The council will receive government funding to pay off 90% of its historic debts accrued through supporting children and young people with SEND, following submission of the SEND Reform Plan in June 2026.
findings.detail: The paper links the funding to the SEND Reform Plan and says it will run alongside the Transformation and Experts at Hand grant, rolling out to September 2030. It does not state the size of the debt or the amount of funding.
findings.matters: Government clearance of historic SEND debt bears directly on high-needs budget pressures that finance directors and lenders are tracking at councils across England.
findings.figures: 90% of historic SEND debts; roll-out to September 2030
findings.quote: to pay off 90% of its historic debts accrued through supporting children and young people with SEND

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q2
findings.headline: The Financial Sustainability and Recovery Strategy, approved by Cabinet on 8 July 2026, sets out an '11-point route map to reduce reliance on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)'.
findings.detail: The paper describes the strategy as part of the draft Medium-Term Financial Plan. The Corporate Plan separately commits the council to 'remove the need for Exceptional Financial Support'.
findings.matters: The 11-point plan is the council's stated route away from EFS, so peers and lenders can measure its progress against it.
findings.figures: 11-point route map; approved 8 July 2026
findings.quote: 11-point route map to reduce reliance on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q2
findings.headline: Cabinet approved in September 2026 the structured closure of the Cornovii company over a period of time, to minimise the council's financial exposure.
findings.detail: The paper says the closure was approved as part of the council's financial considerations and is consistent with the Financial Sustainability and Recovery Strategy. A separate line records that the relationship with Cornovii was decided by Cabinet in September.
findings.matters: A council winding down a company to limit its exposure is a step a finance director, or a lender assessing contingent liabilities, would need to track.
findings.quote: Cabinet in September 2026 approved the structured closure of the Cornovii company over a period of time to minimise the financial exposure to the Council

findings.headline: Capital receipts flexibility, extended to March 2030, has historically funded redundancy costs and transformation investment
findings.detail: The paper says the flexible use of capital receipts is being continued for 2027/28, subject to s151 Officer agreement and reporting through in-year monitoring. It describes the guidance as allowing spend of up to 100% of capital receipts on transformation revenue costs.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts to fund redundancy and transformation costs reduces the receipts left for capital, which bears directly on the shortfall the paper describes.
findings.figures: Guidance extended until March 2030; up to 100% of capital receipts
findings.quote: The Council has historically utilised this flexibility to fund redundancy costs resulting from service redesign and restructure changes and transformation investment.

findings.headline: Council says it will prioritise Council Tax increases up to the maximum allowed to pay the costs of debt from EFS
findings.detail: The paper says the council will need to find offset savings in service costs to balance the budget without further EFS, in addition to prioritising Council Tax increases.
findings.matters: Council Tax set at the maximum to fund EFS debt costs is a funding choice a lender or peer council would want to see in the council's position.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: the Council will be prioritising Council Tax increases up to the maximum allowed and will need to find offset savings in the cost of services

findings.headline: Recruitment and retention is recorded as a concern in the workforce risk
findings.detail: The paper says budget has been applied in 2026/27 to restore capacity previously removed, but recruitment and retention remain a concern. It says capacity may in some cases need to be sought from third parties.
findings.matters: Workforce capacity is the constraint on delivering both the savings and the capital programme, which is a pressure other finance teams would recognise.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: it is recognised that recruitment and retention remains a concern

findings.headline: Paper records an ongoing risk of Government intervention, including appointment of envoys or commissioners
findings.detail: The paper says the risk arises if the council cannot provide assurance that it has a credible strategy to reduce its reliance on EFS, and that the council is aware of intervention in other authorities. It says continued delivery of Improvement Plan outcomes is essential to mitigating the risk.
findings.matters: Government intervention in one council's finances is a precedent other finance officers and lenders would look at for their own authority.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: There remains an ongoing risk of Government intervention, including the appointment of envoys or commissioners

findings.headline: External auditor issued statutory recommendations as part of its 2024/25 annual audit
findings.detail: The paper says the external auditor issued statutory recommendations that cast doubt on the integrity of the Council's value for money arrangements. An updated response was reported to Cabinet and Scrutiny in June 2026, and some recommendations require extensive and ongoing work.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations on value for money are the most serious form of audit finding, and the council's response is what other councils and lenders would track.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: The external auditor felt bound to issue statutory recommendations as part of their annual audit for 2024/25

findings.headline: Council has reported Limited Assurance on its Internal Audit Control Framework for seven years
findings.detail: The paper's risk table records the Limited Assurance opinion as having been reported for seven years, limiting confidence in the standards of governance. It says the Statutory Officers Group, introduced in October 2025, monitors implementation of internal audit recommendations.
findings.matters: A multi-year Limited Assurance opinion on internal controls is an audit weakness that peer finance officers and lenders would weigh when assessing governance.
findings.figures: Seven years of Limited Assurance
findings.quote: The Council has reported Limited Assurance on the Internal Audit Control Framework for seven years, limiting confidence in the standards of governance in place within the organisation.

findings.headline: S106 reserves held at £14.202m at 2025/26 year end, with time-limited payments that could be returned to developers
findings.detail: The paper says each S106 agreement can be time restrictive and could result in payments being returned to the developer if the council does not act on the obligations in time. It says expiry dates are recorded and monitored.
findings.matters: Clawback of time-limited developer contributions is a specific risk to the value of S106 reserves that a finance director would want to see managed.
findings.figures: £14.202m S106 reserves at 25/26 year end
findings.quote: The Council currently holds £14.202m in S106 reserves as at the 25/26 financial year end.

findings.headline: CIL reserves held at £35.086m at Q2 2026/27, of which £28.220m is Local and £6.143m is Strategic
findings.detail: The paper says CIL allocation arrangements are under review, including Place Plan eligibility, prioritisation and deliverability. Projects will not be brought forward through the Capital Programme until that review is complete.
findings.matters: Large unallocated CIL balances under review are a reserve a finance director would track, and the reallocation of them is a governance change other councils also face.
findings.figures: £35.086m total CIL reserves; £28.220m Local; £6.143m Strategic
findings.quote: At Q2 2026/27 there is £35.086m held within the CIL reserves.

findings.headline: Oxon Link Road, Swimming in Shropshire Sundorne, Pride Hill and Maesbury Solar Farm are paused with expenditure to date of £6.088m, £1.91m, £1.530m and £0.133m
findings.detail: The paper says the expenditure already made may need to revert to revenue if these projects do not restart, unless related projects can be substituted. Oxon Link Road is paused following the cancellation of the Northwest Relief Road project.
findings.matters: Capital spent on paused schemes that falls back to revenue would hit the revenue budget directly, which other councils with paused schemes would want to know about.
findings.figures: £6.088m (Oxon Link Road); £1.91m (Sundorne swimming); £1.530m (Pride Hill); £0.133m (Maesbury Solar Farm)
findings.quote: If these projects do not restart, the expenditure to date may need to revert to revenue unless related and relevant projects can be substituted.

findings.headline: Revenue budget is being managed through borrowing under Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)
findings.detail: The paper says the need to use EFS borrowing is a priority to manage the revenue budget. It states that EFS costs of debt for both interest and principal create an additional overhead on the budget.
findings.matters: EFS borrowing is funding revenue spend, which a lender or peer council would see as a different risk from borrowing for capital assets.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: the need to use borrowing through Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) as a priority to manage the revenue budget

findings.headline: Capital receipts are to be used partly to enable consideration of a capitalisation direction request to the Government
findings.detail: The paper says accelerating the disposal programme would allow consideration of a capitalisation direction request, which would convert capital receipts to revenue resources and relieve pressure on revenue budgets, including contributions to General Fund Balances.
findings.matters: A capitalisation direction is a route other councils under financial pressure use to fund revenue costs, and a lender would want to know if the council is relying on one.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: to enable consideration of a capitalisation direction request to the Government to convert capital receipts to revenue resources.

findings.headline: Draft new scheme priorities total £83.305m, with £48.534m proposed from capital receipts and £27.500m from borrowing
findings.detail: Appendix C lists new priority additions over 2027-28 to 2036-37, including Swimming in Shropshire at an estimated £32.000m and leisure maintenance at £12.458m. The paper says these are subject to Council agreement in February 2027.
findings.matters: The new programme leans on the same capital receipts that are already projected to fall short, and adds borrowing, so a lender or peer council would see both the new debt and the receipts dependence.
findings.figures: £83.305m total; £48.534m capital receipts; £27.500m borrowing; £32.000m Swimming in Shropshire; £12.458m leisure maintenance
findings.quote: Total Priority Additions 83.305

findings.headline: Council plans to borrow £2.036m to fund projects already in the capital programme and previously approved
findings.detail: The paper says this borrowing funds current programme commitments. Appendix B shows the same figure as Prudential Borrowing in 2027/28, with no borrowing in 2028/29 or 2029/30 in that appendix.
findings.matters: This is the borrowing the council says it needs now, separate from the larger borrowing that would follow any capital receipts shortfall.
findings.quote: The council is planning to borrow £2.036m to fund projects currently in the capital programme and previously approved.

findings.headline: HRA capital receipts are shown in surplus of £10.851m in 2026/27 and £4.023m in 2027/28, then in shortfall from 2028/29 on the paper's table
findings.detail: The paper's narrative describes the HRA as in a healthy surplus position over the period. Its HRA table, however, shows shortfalls of £1.977m in 2028/29 and £4.977m in each of 2029/30 and 2030/31.
findings.matters: The HRA surplus is presented as offsetting the General Fund gap, so a lender or peer council would need to know it reverses from 2028/29 on the paper's own table.
findings.quote: These tables clearly demonstrate that capital receipts for the HRA are in a healthy surplus position over the period

findings.headline: Capital receipts are projected in surplus by £16.491m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The surplus is split between the General Fund at £5.640m and the HRA at £10.851m in the paper's tables. The paper presents this surplus as the position that mitigates the General Fund shortfall from 2027/28.
findings.matters: This is the only year in the paper's projection with a capital receipts surplus, so it is the cushion a council has before the General Fund gap opens.
findings.figures: £16.491m corporate surplus 2026/27; General Fund £5.640m; HRA £10.851m (tables give £16,491,303, £5,640,250 and £10,851,053)
findings.quote: In 2026/27 there is currently a projected surplus of capital receipts of £16.491m

findings.headline: Larger disposals are described as needing a lead time of at least 12 to 18 months
findings.detail: The paper says considerable work is required to realise the receipts and that larger disposals generally need a lead time of at least 12 to 18 months. It sets this against the commitment to refresh the Asset Management Strategy to minimise the period to achieve each receipt.
findings.matters: A lead time of 12 to 18 months has to be set against shortfalls that start in 2027/28, which is the timing question a finance director would ask of any receipts-funded programme.
findings.figures: 12 to 18 months lead time on larger disposals
findings.quote: Considerable work is required to realise these receipts, with generally a lead in time of at least 12 to 18 months on larger disposals.

findings.headline: Assets under consideration for disposal total £44.903m, which the paper says would cover the projected capital receipts shortfall up to 2028/29
findings.detail: Of the £44.903m, £36.502m is rated Amber and £8.401m Red. The paper describes Amber as achievable but challenging and Red as highly unlikely to complete within the relevant financial years.
findings.matters: The shortfall depends on disposals that are largely not yet rated green, so the timing and realisation of these receipts is what a lender or peer council would need to track.
findings.figures: £44.903m total; £36.502m Amber; £8.401m Red
findings.quote: Assets currently being considered for disposal total £44.903m which if realised would be sufficient to resolve the currently projected shortfall in capital receipts up to 2028/29.

findings.headline: General Fund capital receipts are projected to fall short by cumulative £11.352m in 2027/28, £24.367m in 2028/29 and £33.875m in 2029/30
findings.detail: The paper reports that the General Fund has a projected capital receipts shortfall in each year. It says the shortfall may need to be financed from Prudential Borrowing if it cannot be addressed by progressing the disposals programmed for future years, with revenue costs not budgeted for in the revenue financial strategy.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, would want to see how a council plans to cover a multi-year gap in capital receipts before it turns into borrowing with unbudgeted revenue costs.
findings.quote: In 2027/28, 2028/29 and 2029/30 there are currently projected cumulative shortfalls of capital receipts of £ 11.352m, £24.367m and £33.875m respectively.

findings.headline: Some housing delivery commitments have slipped while the Council awaits the arrival of a new Service Director.
findings.detail: The paper says the Service Director will set milestones so progress can be assessed accurately next quarter. It does not describe the financial effect of the slippage.
findings.matters: A senior vacancy delaying a delivery programme is a leadership change a finance officer elsewhere can compare against their own service planning.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: Some housing delivery commitments have slipped awaiting arrival of the new Service Director

findings.headline: The paper reports 16 red and 1 amber KPIs, the same count as in Quarter 1.
findings.detail: The report says the red and amber KPI count is unchanged from the previous quarter. It names road maintenance, bus connectivity and looked after children as areas below comparator performance.
findings.matters: A flat KPI position across two quarters tells a finance director that performance pressures in statutory and high-cost services are not yet easing.
findings.figures: 16 red KPIs; 1 amber KPI
findings.quote: 16 Red and 1 Amber rated KPI

findings.headline: The paper states that significant management action is required over the remainder of the financial year, and that some performance reductions may be needed to remain within the financial envelope.
findings.detail: The report says it is unlikely that every indicator can reach optimal performance and that some reductions may be needed to stay within the overall financial envelope. It also lists deprioritising service areas as a mitigation for staff capacity risk.
findings.matters: Explicitly accepting lower performance in some services to stay within a fixed envelope is a choice other councils facing the same constraint will be making.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: significant management action required over the remainder of the financial year

findings.headline: The paper says the Council aims to reduce its reliance on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS).
findings.detail: The paper links external scrutiny to the Council's response to its financial challenges and its goal of reducing EFS dependence. It gives no EFS amount or timetable in this report.
findings.matters: EFS reliance is the central question for any lender to a council in this position, and this paper confirms it remains a stated objective without quantifying it.
findings.figures: No EFS amount or timetable given in this paper
findings.quote: reduce its reliance on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)

findings.headline: Since 1 April 2026 the Council has been subject to an independent assurance review carried out by CIPFA on behalf of MHCLG, alongside the External Auditor Annual Value for Money Assessment.
findings.detail: The paper lists these reviews among a range of external reviews since 1 April 2026, which also include a SEND area visit or inspection and an LGA Corporate Peer Challenge follow-up visit. The paper does not give the findings of any of them.
findings.matters: The CIPFA assurance review and the external auditor's value for money assessment are the reviews a finance director elsewhere would expect to read for how this council's financial controls are judged.
findings.figures: None given in the paper
findings.quote: an independent assurance review carried out by CIPFA on behalf of MHCLG

findings.headline: The Council received a Best Value Notice from MHCLG in July 2026.
findings.detail: The paper lists the notice among the external scrutiny the Council has faced since 1 April 2026. It says the Council is a best value authority under the Local Government Act 1999.
findings.matters: A Best Value Notice is a formal central government intervention step, and a lender or peer finance officer would want to know it has been issued.
findings.figures: Best Value Notice received July 2026
findings.quote: the Council received a Best Value Notice from MHCLG

findings.headline: The Q2 report shows 9 of 48 Corporate Plan delivery commitments completed by the end of Quarter 2, with 29 in progress or on track, 5 red and 5 amber.
findings.detail: The report states that the 48 delivery commitments are the basis of quarterly reporting against the Corporate Plan. It also says there are more commitments slipping than in Quarter 1.
findings.matters: A finance director at a peer council can compare how many of Shropshire's transformation and corporate commitments are landing against the pace of its financial sustainability work.
findings.figures: 9 of 48 delivery commitments completed; 29 in progress/on track; 5 red; 5 amber
findings.quote: 9 of the 48 Corporate Plan delivery commitments have been completed by the end of Quarter 2

findings.paper_title: Appendix B Highway Infrastructure Asset Management Strategy Highlighted
findings.headline: The carriageway strategy says reactive repairs drain council resources, and proposes shifting spending toward longer-term investment.
findings.detail: The paper states that reactive repairs should be done 'right first time' and replaced with planned maintenance where most appropriate. It says lifecycle planning will be used to establish a baseline funding requirement for the network.
findings.matters: A stated intention to move spend from reactive to planned work is a budget-shaping decision that a finance director would want to track against actual outturn.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper.
findings.quote: Reactive repairs can be a drain on Council resources, reducing these will enable more longer-term investment in the asset.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B Highway Infrastructure Asset Management Strategy Highlighted
findings.headline: Drainage is funded from revenue rather than capital, and the council has moved from cyclical to reactive maintenance, with limited data on performance.
findings.detail: The paper says the council has moved to a reactive rather than cyclical maintenance regime for drainage, which means there is limited intelligence on how the asset performs. Data on outfall systems is very limited, and a risk-based approach to collecting it has been adopted.
findings.matters: A drainage budget that is revenue-funded and reactive is a different cost profile from a planned capital programme, and a council with limited performance data has less basis for forecasting it.
findings.figures: Around 92,000 gullies and catchpits (Table 1 gives 92,278 in number).
findings.quote: The successful operation of this asset group is ensured by revenue funding rather than capital funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B Highway Infrastructure Asset Management Strategy Highlighted
findings.headline: The council has decided not to complete a full inventory of retaining walls because the cost is prohibitive, and manages them reactively.
findings.detail: The paper says detailed asset data exists for all structure types except retaining walls. The retaining walls will be managed using a reactive regime.
findings.matters: A known gap in asset data that the council has chosen not to close is relevant to how a finance director judges the completeness of the asset valuation and future liability.
findings.figures: Approximately 1,500 walls retaining a height of 1.35m or greater.
findings.quote: The cost of completing the inventory is prohibitive compared to the risk of failure against other priorities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B Highway Infrastructure Asset Management Strategy Highlighted
findings.headline: The bridge stock has an average condition score of 79 (April 2025), and the paper says condition could decline rapidly without maintained funding.
findings.detail: The paper describes the bridge stock as 'fair' and sets a three-year strengthening and replacement forward programme. It warns that funding levels must be kept to avoid an expanded backlog of maintenance and renewal works.
findings.matters: A funding shortfall on structures would turn into a larger future renewal bill, which is a risk for both the council's capital plans and its lenders.
findings.figures: Average condition score of 79 (April 2025); 835 bridges or culverts with a span of 1.5 m or greater; 175 smaller bridges or culverts; approximately 1,500 retaining walls.
findings.quote: Unless the current level of funding is maintained, there is the potential for a rapid decline in bridge condition, leading to an expanded backlog of maintenance and renewal works.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B Highway Infrastructure Asset Management Strategy Highlighted
findings.headline: The carriageway strategy records more than 12% of roads as 'functionally impaired', with more than 17% of C roads in that condition.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the condition to years of under-funding and says customer satisfaction with carriageway maintenance is low. It states that reactive repairs can drain council resources and that reducing them would allow more long-term investment.
findings.matters: The paper links the current road condition directly to past funding levels, which bears on how much backlog a council carries into its next capital programme.
findings.figures: More than 12% of roads functionally impaired; more than 17% of C roads could be functionally impaired; 5,168 km of carriageway.
findings.quote: More than 12% of roads have deteriorated to a stage that they are ‘functionally impaired’.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B Highway Infrastructure Asset Management Strategy Highlighted
findings.headline: The strategy describes the DfT Incentive Element for 2025/26 to 2029/30 as conditional funding and 'a significant proportion of the overall available investment'.
findings.detail: The paper states that the Incentive Element is conditional on criteria local highway authorities must meet. It lists 'Maximising the available funding for highways maintenance by meeting the Department for Transport's Incentive Fund criteria' as a priority under Priority 2.
findings.matters: A large share of highway maintenance funding depends on meeting DfT criteria, so a finance director here or at another council would want to know how much of the budget is at risk if those criteria are missed.
findings.figures: None stated in the paper.
findings.quote: The ‘Incentive Element’ of funding is conditional on criteria that must be met by local highway authorities and is a significant proportion of the overall available investment

findings.headline: Transformation funding proposals stand at approximately £3.532m for 2026/27 and over £11m for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper says the current base budget includes £10m to invest in transformation, which is effectively a revenue resource made possible through EFS. It notes that not all projects are expected to save money, as some represent the rebuilding of council capacity.
findings.matters: Using EFS to fund transformation spend, rather than savings already delivered, is a model other councils with EFS dependence will be assessing.
findings.figures: £10m (base budget transformation provision); £3.532m (2026/27 proposals); over £11m (2027/28 proposals)
findings.quote: The proposals for funding in 2026/27 is currently standing at approximately £3.532m and at over £11m for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Cabinet will not continue the 'Commissioning Council' policy adopted in 2018, and the climate strategy is to be suspended.
findings.detail: The paper says these legacy policies are no longer appropriate in the current financial position. It also says the climate strategy is outdated and not in line with national policy and other councils, and the paper recommends suspending it and presenting an affordable updated strategy.
findings.matters: Changes to a council's operating model and its policy commitments are the kind of decision that affects how transformation and savings are delivered.
findings.figures: 2018 (year the policy was adopted)
findings.quote: That Cabinet will not be continuing with the previous policy of being a ‘Commissioning Council’ adopted in 2018

findings.headline: External auditors have highlighted the low level of balances held in reference to the Council's financial resilience.
findings.detail: The paper also records that the Council has reported Limited Assurance on its internal audit control framework for seven years. It says the external auditor issued statutory recommendations on the 2024/25 value for money arrangements, and that an updated response was reported to scrutiny and Cabinet in June 2026.
findings.matters: Repeated limited audit assurance and statutory recommendations on value for money are signals that finance directors and lenders use to judge governance.
findings.figures: seven years (limited internal audit assurance); £59.672m to £34.814m (total reserves over three years)
findings.quote: The low level of balances held has been highlighted by our external auditors in reference to the financial resilience of the Council.

findings.headline: The paper says that without the 2026/27 EFS the Council would have been unable to set a balanced budget and the s151 Officer would have had to issue a s114 notice.
findings.detail: The paper states that the EFS was essential to restabilise the budget, filling structural deficits in adults' and children's social care and removing unachievable savings targets from the base. It also says there is an ongoing risk of Government intervention, including envoys or commissioners, if the council cannot show a credible strategy to reduce EFS reliance.
findings.matters: A s114 notice and government intervention are the outcomes lenders and finance directors most closely track, and the paper says both remain possible risks.
findings.figures: £121m (EFS approved in principle, 2026/27); £71m (EFS for 2025/26)
findings.quote: Ultimately, without this EFS, the Council would have been unable to set a balanced budget for the year and it would have been necessary for the s151 Officer to issue a s114 notice.

findings.headline: A best-case model assumes an 8.99% council tax increase, above the 4.99% cap, which would take Band D to £2,146.11.
findings.detail: The paper says the increase would raise £9.741m and reduce the 2027/28 EFS requirement to £97.375m, and that any rise above the cap needs explicit agreement from MHCLG. Each 1% on council tax is said to raise about £2.4m. The Section 151 Officer will recommend raising council tax to the maximum possible level if dispensation is given.
findings.matters: Council tax flexibility above the cap is a lever other councils with EFS are also seeking, and the uplift is a direct offset to the gap.
findings.figures: £1,969.09 (Band D, 2026/27); £2,146.11 (Band D with 8.99%); 8.99% (best-case increase); 4.99% (cap); £9.741m (additional income); £97.375m (revised EFS requirement, 2027/28); £2.4m (per 1%)
findings.quote: The best-case model includes an increase of 8.99% which would bring the Band D Council Tax to £2,146.11

findings.matters: A finance director would track how much of a transformation provision is committed at halfway and what happens to any unallocated balance.

findings.matters: A seven-year run of limited assurance and statutory external audit recommendations is a governance position any lender or peer finance director would weigh.

findings.paper_title: 20260925 Internal Audit Performance Report - Appendix A-09092026 1701
findings.headline: Improvement in audit assurance (58% Good/Reasonable vs 35% prior year) but based on small sample of 29 audits; paper warns against interpreting as statistically significant
findings.detail: 17 of 29 audits received Good or Reasonable assurance (58%), compared to 35% in the same period 2025/26. However, the audit team explicitly cautions: 'given the relatively small number of completed audits at this stage of the year, this movement should be interpreted with caution and should not, at this point, be regarded as evidence of a statistically significant change in the overall control environment.'
findings.matters: Prevents misreading of improvement trend; reader should know that apparent 58% improvement is unreliable and the underlying control position remains unclear.
findings.figures: 17 of 29 reports Good/Reasonable (58%); 12 Limited/Unsatisfactory (42%)
findings.quote: given the relatively small number of completed audits at this stage of the year, this movement should be interpreted with caution and should not, at this point, be regarded as evidence of a statistically significant change in the overall control environment.

findings.paper_title: 20260925 Internal Audit Performance Report - Appendix A-09092026 1701
findings.headline: Audit staffing loss: Principal and Senior Auditor resignations lead to 377-day reduction in approved audit plan; recruitment restart underway
findings.detail: Two key audit staff resigned; initial recruitment campaign in March 2026 was unsuccessful. The revised 2026/27 audit plan reduces to 2,025 days from the originally approved total, a cut of 377 days. New recruitment campaign is currently underway. This reduction occurs at a time when audit work is identifying control weaknesses across multiple service areas.
findings.matters: Reduced internal audit capacity means less oversight of the control environment at a time when audits are flagging systemic governance gaps.
findings.figures: 377 days reduction; revised plan 2,025 days
findings.quote: Changes to the planned activity are required following the resignation of a Principal and Senior Auditor.

findings.paper_title: 20260925 Internal Audit Performance Report - Appendix A-09092026 1701
findings.headline: 54% of prior audit recommendations remain only partially implemented or have been repeated; control improvements not embedded
findings.detail: Follow-up review of recommendation status found that 54% of reviewed prior actions 'remained only partially implemented or had been repeated,' with 228 actions closed on management assurance alone without independent audit verification. This demonstrates that formal closure of recommendations does not equate to actual embedding of improved controls.
findings.matters: If prior recommendations are not genuinely being implemented, the apparent improvement in current audit assurance (58% Good/Reasonable) may be illusory and controls are not actually strengthening.
findings.figures: 54% of reviewed actions partially implemented or repeated; 228 actions closed without verification

findings.paper_title: UPDATED REPORT - Financial Monitoring Report Quarter 1 2026.27-02072026 1235 v8
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit of £46.283m, managed under statutory override through March 2028.
findings.detail: The in-year DSG deficit is £40.727m. Combined with the carried-forward deficit from 2025/26, the cumulative position is £46.283m (anticipated after 90% write-off via High Needs Stability Grant of £41.090m). The deficit is being managed through a statutory override agreed nationally for DSG deficits through March 2028. Main pressures are top-up funding to mainstream schools and SEND hubs (£34.843m of the in-year deficit) and growth in independent placements.
findings.matters: The DSG is ring-fenced by law but the statutory override is temporary (expires March 2028). If the council cannot reduce its SEND demand trajectory or is not granted further relief, it will face a cliff-edge funding problem when the override ends. This is a structural demand issue, not a one-off.
findings.figures: In-year DSG deficit £40.727m; cumulative deficit £46.283m (anticipated); High Needs Stability Grant £41.090m; override expires March 2028; three spending areas account for £34.843m: top-ups to mainstream and hubs, increases to state-funded special schools, growth in independent providers.
findings.quote: It should be noted that this figure is the in-year deficit and needs to be added to the deficit carried forward from 2025-26 in order to give an overall forecast cumulative DSG deficit position of £46.283m...
