findings.detail: The council reports sickness absence levels continue to exceed target, with anxiety, stress, depression and related illness identified as the main drivers. The Improvement Plan addresses this through the People Plan, though the document notes this area requires sustained attention.
findings.matters: Elevated mental health-related sickness absence signals workforce stress and operational resilience concerns, potentially driving higher agency staffing costs and impacting service continuity.
findings.figures: Sickness absence above target (extent not quantified); anxiety/stress/depression identified as main cause
findings.quote: sickness absence remains above target, with anxiety, stress, depression and related illness the main cause

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q1
findings.headline: Council is executing a phased asset disposal programme to generate capital receipts supporting financial strategy
findings.detail: The council has commenced its first phase of planned asset disposals to generate capital receipts underpinning the Financial Sustainability and Recovery Strategy. Disposal of St Andrews in Shifnal has been completed, with further major strategic asset decisions on Shirehall, Oswestry SUE Corner Site, and Whitchurch Civic Centre & Library scheduled for Q2.
findings.matters: Asset disposal proceeds and capital receipts are material components of the council's financial strategy; visibility on planned disposals provides insight into balance sheet management and future capital availability.
findings.figures: St Andrews (Shifnal) disposal completed; three major assets under review in Q2 2026/27
findings.quote: the first phase of asset disposals is generating capital receipts to support the Financial Sustainability and Recovery Strategy, including decisions such as the disposal of St Andrews in Shifnal

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q1
findings.headline: Council has adopted an 11-point Financial Sustainability and Recovery Strategy to reduce reliance on Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The council approved a Financial Sustainability and Recovery Strategy in July 2026 as part of its draft Medium-Term Financial Plan for 2027/28–2031/32. The strategy comprises an 11-point route map specifically designed to reduce dependence on Exceptional Financial Support over the medium term.
findings.matters: Reducing reliance on EFS is a critical financial sustainability metric; the existence of a multi-year structured plan indicates the council recognises financial vulnerabilities and is implementing systematic measures to address them.
findings.figures: 11-point route map; MTFP period 2027/28–2031/32; current EFS reliance (amount unspecified)
findings.quote: Our Financial Sustainability and Recovery Strategy was approved by 8 July 2026 Cabinet as part of the draft Medium-Term Financial Plan 2027/28 – 2031/32, setting out our 11-point route map to achieve this and reducing reliance on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan Performance Report Q1
findings.headline: First quarter shows forecast underspend of £2.291m with £5.238m in savings already achieved, exceeding the £5m target
findings.detail: The council reports positive Q1 financial performance with a forecast general fund underspend of £2.291m and savings of £5.238m already forecast to be achieved. This exceeds the annual £5m savings target, with a further £523k still to be delivered by March 2027.
findings.matters: Consistent in-year savings delivery is a key indicator of financial discipline and budget control, essential for assessing the council's capacity to service debt and meet financial commitments.
findings.figures: £2.291m underspend; £5.238m savings achieved against £5m target; £523k to deliver
findings.quote: Early financial performance is positive, with a forecast underspend of £2.291m against the general fund budget and savings of £5.238m already forecast to be achieved, exceeding the £5m target for 2026/27, with a further £523k still to be delivered by March 2027.

findings.headline: Council states "significant management action required over the remainder of the financial year to ensure the Council's financial survival"
findings.detail: In the risk and opportunities section, the document explicitly frames the council's financial position as requiring significant action to ensure survival. It notes the council may need to prioritise some strategic objectives over others and accept reductions in performance in some areas to remain within the financial envelope.
findings.matters: The language of 'financial survival' signals acute financial stress; the council is not describing financial challenge but existential financial risk requiring urgent action.
findings.figures: Described as requiring 'significant management action' but no quantified target
findings.quote: significant management action required over the remainder of the financial year to ensure the Council's financial survival

findings.headline: Council identifies staff capacity as a key risk to maintaining service provision and completing transformation
findings.detail: The risk register explicitly flags 'Staff capacity to maintain levels of service provision and deliver the transformation required' as a live risk, with mitigations including deprioritising service areas, identifying functions and roles as gaps, and managing expectations about service changes.
findings.matters: Staff capacity constraints indicate the council may struggle to deliver both current services and the transformation programme needed to address financial sustainability; this is a delivery risk.
findings.figures: Not quantified; identified as strategic risk requiring mitigation
findings.quote: Staff capacity to maintain levels of service provision. And deliver the transformation required.

findings.headline: Six KPIs showing worsening performance (red direction of travel) and 34 showing stagnation (amber)
findings.detail: Out of 53 KPIs tracked across the Corporate Plan, only 13 show improvement (green), 34 show stagnation or required attention (amber), and 6 show deteriorating performance (red). The council notes this context: "it may not be possible to achieve optimal performance across all indicators and it may be necessary to oversee expected reductions in performance in some areas."
findings.matters: Deteriorating KPI performance across multiple service areas signals operational stress; the council is explicitly accepting performance declines as it manages financial constraints.
findings.figures: 13 green (improving), 34 amber (stagnant), 6 red (worsening) out of 53 KPIs
findings.quote: The majority of the KPIs performance is being maintained at a similar level to the previous reporting period... Performance is worsening (6 red arrows)

findings.headline: Q1 forecast shows underspend of £2.291m but within a recovery strategy context
findings.detail: Financial monitoring identified a £2.291m underspend at Q1. However, this is occurring within the council's Financial Sustainability and Recovery Strategy, suggesting underspends may reflect reduced activity or deferred spending rather than operational efficiency.
findings.matters: While a Q1 underspend appears positive, it must be read against the council's stated need for transformation and cost reduction; underspends can mask deteriorating service delivery or deferred commitments.
findings.figures: £2.291m forecast underspend Q1
findings.quote: Financial monitoring identifies a forecast underspend of £2.291m at quarter 1

findings.headline: Cabinet closed Helena Lane Older People Day Service and closed the Aquamira building, transferring its service
findings.detail: The council made explicit service reduction decisions in adult social care during Q1, closing an older people day service and consolidating another to a different site. These are active reductions in service provision.
findings.matters: Service closures are a proxy for financial pressure and service demand reduction; they signal the council is actively managing down activity rather than maintaining existing commitments.
findings.figures: 2 service closures/consolidations in adult social care
findings.quote: Cabinet took the difficult decision to close Helena Lane Older People Day Service and transfer the Aquamira Day Service to the Abbots Wood site and close the Aquamira building.

findings.headline: Council continues to rely on Exceptional Financial Support and is working to reduce dependence on it
findings.detail: The council is pursuing a Financial Sustainability and Recovery Strategy explicitly to reduce reliance on EFS. This indicates the council cannot balance its budget from its own resources and requires central government support to operate.
findings.matters: EFS dependence is a structural weakness; it means the council cannot fund its baseline operations and carries elevated refinancing risk for any borrowing.
findings.figures: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) ongoing; reduction target not quantified
findings.quote: it continues to respond to the financial challenges and reduce its reliance on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)

findings.headline: Council received a formal Best Value Notice from MHCLG in July 2026
findings.detail: The document notes the council is subject to significant external scrutiny including a CIPFA assurance review, SEND inspection, LGA follow-up visit, and annual Value for Money Assessment. The Best Value Notice is a formal compliance intervention triggered by financial difficulties and governance concerns.
findings.matters: A Best Value Notice is a serious marker for lenders; it signals regulatory intervention and formal governance weakness in a council already dependent on exceptional financial support.
findings.figures: Best Value Notice issued July 2026
findings.quote: In July 2026 the Council received a Best Value Notice from MHCLG.

findings.headline: £13.1m Whitchurch Swimming & Leisure Facility entering main construction phase in 2026-27 with 40-year financing
findings.detail: Approved September 2022, with £13.08m budgeted for construction in 2026-27 (the main spend phase) and £22k remaining in 2027-28. Debt repayment period of 40 years extends to 2065-66, creating a long-term revenue commitment.
findings.matters: Major leisure facility investment carries operational revenue risk if usage or operating costs diverge from the business case. The 40-year repayment term implies the council is committing its revenue budget to this facility for four decades. Underperforming leisure operations can drain reserves.
findings.figures: £13.1m total approved, £13.08m budgeted 2026-27

findings.headline: Transformation programme borrowing approved at £26.8m (2024-25), £61.9m (2025-26), and £121m (2026-27), representing 44% of total 2026-27 capital spend
findings.detail: Approved transformation spending funded through capital borrowing escalates from £26.8m (2024-25) to £61.9m (2025-26) to £121m (2026-27). All three years are approved under the council's EFS framework. This represents 44% of the council's total budgeted capital spend in 2026-27.
findings.matters: Financing operational transformation costs through capital borrowing indicates the council cannot fund them from revenue. Lenders assess whether councils have revenue headroom to service debt; escalating transformation borrowing raises questions about underlying budget pressure and whether transformation spending will deliver the promised savings.
findings.quote: Transformation Programme 2026-27 Expenditure Funded Through Borrowing Under EFS Approval 121,000,000 0 121,000,000

findings.headline: Crisis Resilience Fund support to claimants continues through 2028-29 at £80 (2026-27), £90 (2027-28), £100 (2028-29) per claimant
findings.detail: Since 2020 the council has used temporary grants to support claimants affected by the 20% minimum payment requirement. From 2026-27 this continues from the Crisis Resilience Fund at rising levels: £80 per claimant in 2026-27, £90 in 2027-28, and £100 in 2028-29. The paper notes claimants 'have not had to pay their council tax liability in full' due to this ongoing support.
findings.matters: A lender needs to track how long reserves can sustain escalating support commitments and what happens when temporary funding ends.
findings.quote: Continue to support those impacted by 20% minimum payment with a top up from the Crisis Resilience Fund as follows: 2026-27 (current year) – up to £80; 2027-28 – up to £90; 2028-29 – up to £100

findings.headline: New recurring cost of £750k-£800k for Child Benefit disregard must be incorporated into MTFP
findings.detail: The council proposes disregarding Child Benefit as income when calculating Council Tax Support from 2027-28. This policy change has an estimated annual cost of £750k to £800k. The financial implications section states this cost 'will need to be incorporated within the MTFP, next due for review by Cabinet in November' but does not identify the funding source.
findings.matters: A lender tracking budget pressures needs to know about new committed expenditure, particularly when the funding source has not been resolved and must be absorbed into MTFP planning.
findings.figures: £750k-£800k per year
findings.quote: Estimated cost of disregarding child benefit as an income is between £750k and £800k and this will need to be incorporated within the MTFP, next due for review by Cabinet in November.

findings.paper_title: Shropshire EFS External Assurance Review - MHCLG.CIPFA Report-07082026 1445
findings.headline: Recovery pace a key risk: council must transform and save while maintaining statutory service delivery
findings.detail: The council identifies its principal risk as 'the pace at which financial recovery and transformation activity can be delivered whilst maintaining service delivery and meeting statutory responsibilities.' It is developing transformation plans for Children's Services, Adult Social Care, Assets, and a Digital Roadmap, but several remain in early stages of development.
findings.matters: A lender assessing whether the council can execute its recovery plan needs to understand capacity constraints and the risk of service failure or missed statutory duties during transformation.
findings.figures: Review undertaken April 2026; progress update due to MHCLG by end September 2026
findings.quote: The principal risk remains the pace at which financial recovery and transformation activity can be delivered whilst maintaining service delivery and meeting statutory responsibilities

findings.paper_title: Shropshire EFS External Assurance Review - MHCLG.CIPFA Report-07082026 1445
findings.headline: CIPFA review identifies significant risks to financial sustainability and organisational capacity
findings.detail: The April 2026 CIPFA assurance review identified significant challenges and made 22 recommendations. The paper states: 'The External Assurance Review highlights significant risks relating to financial sustainability, organisational capacity, transformation delivery and governance.' The council acknowledges several recommendations require 'substantial further work' including detailed transformation plans and quantified savings trajectories.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has adequate financial buffers and whether recovery plans are substantive or still being developed.
findings.figures: 22 recommendations; review conducted April 2026
findings.quote: The External Assurance Review highlights significant risks relating to financial sustainability, organisational capacity, transformation delivery and governance

findings.paper_title: Shropshire EFS External Assurance Review - MHCLG.CIPFA Report-07082026 1445
findings.headline: Council declared financial emergency in September 2025 and is receiving Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: Shropshire is receiving Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from government and is subject to a Best Value Notice process. The council declared a financial emergency in September 2025 and has established an independently-chaired Improvement Board to oversee recovery. MHCLG will monitor implementation of recommendations quarterly.
findings.matters: EFS and Best Value Notice indicate systemic financial distress requiring government intervention; a lender needs to understand the depth of the council's difficulty and the degree of external oversight.
findings.figures: 22 recommendations across financial management, financial sustainability, service transformation and governance
findings.quote: declaration of a financial emergency in September 2025, including the development of an Improvement Plan, establishment of an independently chaired Improvement Board, strengthened governance and compliance arrangements

findings.paper_title: Business Rate Relief and Council Tax Discretionary Discount Policy-10072026 1448
findings.headline: Council cannot expand discretionary support schemes and is creating new exceptional-cases fund due to financial emergency
findings.detail: Cabinet is declining to extend council tax discretionary discounts to residents fleeing domestic abuse, terminally ill taxpayers, child adopters, or emergency service workers, citing inability to estimate costs and lack of available funds. The council is instead creating a new Council Tax Discretionary Discount Hardship Fund to handle exceptional cases outside the agreed policy, to be funded within the Medium Term Financial Plan reviewed in November 2026. The paper states the council is 'not in a financial position to consider further discretionary awards at this time in the context of the financial emergency.'
findings.matters: The council is constrained from expanding even modest discretionary support schemes, and is creating new exception-handling structures to manage demand it cannot accommodate within the main framework. This reflects the severity of financial pressure on spending decisions.
findings.figures: Discretionary business rate relief cost £437k to council in 2025-26 (49% of £891k total); council tax discretionary discounts to care leavers cost £82k
findings.quote: The Council is not in a financial position to consider further discretionary awards at this time in the context of the financial emergency.

findings.headline: Council proposing £750k–£800k annual additional cost for Council Tax Support Scheme changes from 2027
findings.detail: Shropshire is consulting on disregarding child benefit as income when calculating council tax support for working-age residents, reversing a 2013 decision that removed this disregard. The estimated annual cost of this change is £750k to £800k.
findings.matters: A material recurring annual cost commitment of this scale must be accommodated within the medium-term financial strategy and requires funding through savings, income, or reserves.
findings.figures: £750k to £800k per year
findings.quote: The estimated cost of this change is £750k to £800k per year.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased significantly from £352m to £602m (71% increase)
findings.detail: The capital financing requirement has risen materially to £602m from £352m. This drives gross borrowing from £455m to £738m (62% increase), with the council now using £738m of its £929m authorised borrowing limit. The HRA CFR also increased from £103m to £136m.
findings.matters: A material increase in capital financing requirement and gross borrowing is significant to lenders and finance directors, signalling expanded capital spending or revised borrowing assumptions
findings.figures: Non-HRA CFR £602m vs £352m; Gross borrowing £738m vs £455m; HRA CFR £136m vs £103m; Authorised limit £929m
findings.quote: Non HRA Capital Financing Requirement (CFR)  602 352; Gross borrowing   738 455

findings.headline: Future borrowing for Cornovii Developments Limited contingent on Cabinet decision being made at this meeting
findings.detail: The Treasury Management strategy includes borrowing for Cornovii Developments Limited, a wholly owned council company, but a Cabinet report considered alongside this treasury update will determine the company's future. The council states that 'future borrowing forecasts will be amended accordingly' based on that decision, meaning the forward borrowing plan is incomplete.
findings.matters: Uncertainty about a material component of planned borrowing means the council's capital and debt commitments are not yet finalized. Lenders need clarity on actual forward borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: Amount not quantified in this report
findings.quote: Subject to Cabinet's approval to the recommendations in that report, future borrowing forecasts will be amended accordingly.

findings.headline: Council secured £35m temporary borrowing from other councils, betting that PWLB rates will fall
findings.detail: Rather than long-term PWLB borrowing, Shropshire secured £35m in temporary borrowing from other local authorities in Q1, anticipated to mature within 2026/27. This is a tactical interest-rate bet: if PWLB rates fall as expected, this saves cost; if they rise, refinancing could be expensive.
findings.matters: Creates refinancing risk if interest rate forecasts prove incorrect. Lenders would want to know if the council is taking directional bets on rates rather than securing long-term fixed costs.
findings.figures: £35m temporary borrowing
findings.quote: the Council has secured temporary borrowing from other local authorities during Quarter 1 rather than long term PWLB borrowing. As at 30th June, the Council has secured £35m which are anticipated to mature before the end of the 2026/27 financial year.

findings.headline: Reserves have declined, forcing external borrowing; only £22.7m in investments against £455m of debt
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that reserves and cash balances have declined over recent years, making external borrowing necessary. At 30 June 2026, the council held only £22.7m in investments against £455m of outstanding borrowing at fixed rates. This tight liquidity position relative to debt burden represents a significant structural vulnerability.
findings.matters: Thin reserves and high leverage reduce financial flexibility and increase refinancing risk if the council faces unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls.
findings.figures: £22.7m investments, £455m borrowing, average £54.6m available for investment in Q1
findings.quote: As cash balances and reserves at the Council have reduced over recent years it is now necessary to take out new external borrowing

findings.headline: Council requires £121m Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27 to support revenue budget
findings.detail: The council depends on government Exceptional Financial Support to fund its revenue budget in 2026/27. While a revised reserves strategy may reduce this amount, £121m remains approved in principle, indicating the council cannot balance its budget from its own resources.
findings.matters: EFS indicates the council cannot fund its revenue budget without government financial support, a significant credit weakness for lenders evaluating municipal creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £121m approved in principle for 2026/27
findings.quote: During 2026/27, the Council will have a need to borrow, specifically in relation to the Exceptional Financial Support of £121m approved in principle for 2026/27 to support the revenue budget

findings.headline: Council is maxing out Council Tax increases and considering deprioritising carbon neutral 2030 target 'given the financial emergency facing the Council'
findings.detail: The council states it is 'prioritising Council Tax increases up to the maximum allowed' to offset government funding reductions. It is now reconsidering its carbon neutral 2030 target, noting 'This original target is now well in advance of government and other local authority targets and most be reviewed closely given the financial emergency facing the Council.' Commercial activities (Cornovii Developments Ltd and pyrolysis joint venture) are also under review.
findings.matters: Maxed-out Council Tax removes a key fiscal lever for future years. The decision to reconsider environmental commitments signals the council views itself in sufficient financial distress to deprioritise non-statutory objectives. For a lender, this is a signal of financial pressure and constrained choices.
findings.figures: Council Tax at maximum allowed increase; carbon neutral target for 2030 under review
findings.quote: The pyroloysis review will also allow for a review of the reality of the Council's carbon neutral target for 2030. This original target is now well in advance of government and other local authority targets and most be reviewed closely given the financial emergency facing the Council.

findings.headline: Savings delivery 90.92% on track; £523k shortfall includes unconfirmed ICB/CHC income recovery of £375k
findings.detail: £5.238m of £5.761m target savings are forecast delivered. Outstanding items include: ICB/CHC income (£375k, forecast not achieved but 'detailed review in period 4 may fully mitigate'); Libraries (£93k pending consultation on future delivery); Museums (£50k review commissioned); and ceremonies income (£5k at risk). The ICB/CHC item depends on a 'detailed review of all income sources' that has not yet concluded.
findings.matters: If the £523k shortfall is not delivered, it will require alternative funding or reserves draw. The largest item (£375k) is contingent on an income review not yet complete. This creates real downside risk to the forecast.
findings.figures: £5.238m delivered against £5.761m target (90.92%); £523k shortfall, of which £375k is contingent on future income review
findings.quote: CW002 – ICB/CHC £375k: This saving relates mainly to increased CHC income. At Quarter 1, the forecast assumes the saving will not be achieved. However, a detailed review of all income sources is taking place in period 4, which indicates the saving may be fully mitigated through wider income improvements.

findings.headline: Projected capital receipts shortfalls: £19.863m (2027/28), £30.408m (2028/29), £39.916m (2029/30)
findings.detail: The capital programme relies heavily on capital receipts. General Fund faces projected shortfalls of £19.863m, £30.408m and £39.916m in outer years. Assets currently considered for disposal total £41.553m, but 'if realised will still fall short of the total capital receipts required'. The council notes these shortfalls 'will be financed from Prudential Borrowing' and that disposals have 'generally a lead in time of at least 12 to 18 months on larger disposals'.
findings.matters: If capital receipts do not materialise, the council will need to increase borrowing or reduce the capital programme. Either option weakens financial flexibility. The fact that even all disposals currently identified fall short suggests the capital strategy is not yet robust.
findings.figures: Shortfalls: £19.863m (2027/28), £30.408m (2028/29), £39.916m (2029/30); assets for disposal total £41.553m but still insufficient
findings.quote: Assets currently being considered for disposal total £41.553m which if realised will still fall short of the total capital receipts required within the capital programme. It is therefore necessary for the asset base to be reviewed in detail to identify further assets that can be considered for disposal.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit of £46.283m, managed through statutory override until March 2028
findings.detail: The in-year DSG deficit is £40.727m; combined with brought-forward deficit this totals £46.283m. Three areas account for £34.843m of overspend: top-up funding to mainstream schools and SEND hubs, state-funded special school top-ups, and growth in independent provider placements. This is managed through a Statutory Override which expires 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: The statutory override masking this £46.283m structural deficit expires in 2028. The council must develop a credible plan to address this before override expiry, or the gap will hit the general fund. This is a known obligation the council must manage.
findings.figures: £46.283m cumulative DSG deficit (£40.727m in-year); £34.843m in three main overspend areas
findings.quote: The overall 2026-27 outturn against centrally retained DSG is forecast to be £40.727m in deficit as at the end of June 2026. It should be noted that this figure is the in-year deficit and needs to be added to the deficit carried forward from 2025-26.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support requirement of £90m (down from £121m in February), but still substantial government support dependency
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 budget relies on £90m in Exceptional Financial Support, a reduction of £31m from the February MTFP. EFS carries additional debt servicing costs beyond normal inflation. MHCLG reviews 'will be seeking evidence of improvement against their report recommendations and of progressive reductions in the Council's requirements for EFS'.
findings.matters: The council still needs £90m in exceptional support, signalling ongoing structural imbalance. The regulator expects 'progressive reductions', putting pressure on future budget capacity. Debt servicing costs on EFS add permanent overhead.
findings.figures: £90m EFS for 2026/27 (£31m reduction from £121m in February MTFP)
findings.quote: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) incurs costs of debt for both interest and principal of a fixed number of years and creates an additional overhead over and above the costs of additional demands for services.

findings.headline: Seven consecutive years of Limited Assurance on Internal Audit Control Framework; external auditor issued statutory recommendations
findings.detail: The council's control environment has been rated Limited Assurance for seven years. The external auditor issued statutory recommendations for 2024/25 'casting doubt on the integrity of the Council's value for money arrangements'. A Non-Statutory Best Value Notice has been issued and MHCLG reviews begin in September 2026, seeking 'evidence of improvement against their report recommendations'.
findings.matters: Seven years of Limited Assurance represents sustained weakness in the control framework. The regulator (MHCLG) has now intervened with a Best Value Notice. For a lender, this raises material questions about financial reporting reliability and management competence.
findings.figures: Seven consecutive years at Limited Assurance; statutory recommendations issued for 2024/25
findings.quote: The Council has reported Limited Assurance on the Internal Audit Control Framework for seven years, limiting confidence in the standards of governance in place within the organisation.

findings.headline: Children's social care overspend of £3.285m, with £2m identified as unbudgeted pressures after budget-setting
findings.detail: The child care budget of £44m is forecast to overspend by £3.285m. External residential placements are the largest driver, caused by a sufficiency deficit in foster placements, especially for children with complex needs. Mitigations (9 step-downs, 4 aging out for £2.325m combined) have been offset by new placements and escalating needs. The s151 officer has flagged this as 'the largest risk to the delivery of the Council's budget'.
findings.matters: Children's social care is the dominant budget risk. A lender must assess whether the council can contain this £3.285m or whether it will grow and consume reserves or require further EFS in future years.
findings.figures: £3.285m overspend on £44m child care budget; £2m is unbudgeted post-setting; £2.325m saved from step-downs and aging out
findings.quote: The budget for the care of children is £44 million but projecting an overspend of £3.285m. The single largest contributing factor is the increase in External Residential placements and related costs.

findings.headline: Capital delivery dependent on securing external grant funding Homes England bids not yet approved
findings.detail: The Business Plan 'supports potential applications for Government grant funding to increase capacity within the HRA stock,' but the document explicitly notes 'This does not constitute approval to submit a bid.' Grant funding is described as 'central to maximising the delivery of new affordable, specialist and supported housing while reducing the level of borrowing or HRA resources required.' Without grant wins, the council will need to rely more heavily on reserves or borrowing.
findings.matters: The HRA's capital ambitions (new build, stock expansion, specialist housing) are contingent on competitive bids that have not yet been approved or even submitted. Failure to secure grants would force trade-offs between borrowing, reserve depletion, or reduced delivery.
findings.figures: Provision made within plan; specific schemes and amounts not yet defined pending bid decisions
findings.quote: Provision has been made within the HRA Business Plan to support potential applications for Government grant funding to increase capacity within the HRA stock. This does not constitute approval to submit a bid. A further detailed report will be brought back to Cabinet for consideration and approval before any bid is submitted.

findings.headline: HRA 30-year Business Plan delayed from February 2026 to September 2026 due to General Fund financial uncertainties
findings.detail: The 30-year Business Plan, due in February 2026, was delayed due to 'uncertainties regarding policy priorities and timing and wider concern for Council finances.' This is the HRA's core planning document—the delay indicates the General Fund crisis is actively disrupting HRA planning cycles.
findings.matters: A delayed HRA plan means the council lacked a current forward financial model during its financial emergency period, and may indicate weakness in long-term treasury management discipline.
findings.figures: Plan delayed from February 2026 to September 2026
findings.quote: The Plan was due to be brought forward in February 2026 but was delayed given uncertainties regarding policy priorities and timing and wider concern for Council finances.

findings.headline: Independent review found governance and reserves policy gaps in HRA management
findings.detail: An independent HRA review undertaken in June 2026 found the account is 'currently in a sound position' but identified weaknesses in financial governance, reserves policy, borrowing assumptions, viability assessment and oversight arrangements. These gaps were significant enough to trigger development of a new HRA Policy and suggest prior control failures. The review was necessitated partly by the council's General Fund distress.
findings.matters: Pre-existing governance gaps on reserves management and viability assessment indicate previous oversight failures, raising questions about whether the new policy framework will hold under stress or during the next leadership change.
findings.figures: 30-year business plan subject to independent review and scenario testing
findings.quote: An independent review of the HRA undertaken in June 2026 found that the HRA is currently in a sound position but it did identify areas where financial governance, reserves policy, borrowing assumptions, viability assessment and oversight arrangements should be strengthened.

findings.headline: General Fund financial emergency is now constraining HRA borrowing decisions
findings.detail: Shropshire declared a financial emergency on 10 September 2025 across the General Fund. The £174m HRA borrowing cap agreed in February 2025 is now under explicit review by Cabinet, with the document stating it 'will remain under scrutiny from Cabinet moving forward and subject to decisions as part of the Capital Strategy, not least given the increasing level of regulatory compliance brought in by central government and the Council's current financial situation.' The Council's wider financial distress is directly shaping HRA capacity.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether HRA borrowing headroom is being crowded out by General Fund pressures, and whether the council can sustain its planned £174m debt load if the financial emergency worsens.
findings.figures: £174 million borrowing cap (agreed February 2025, now under review)
findings.quote: Shropshire Council continues to manage unprecedented financial demands, and a financial emergency was declared by Cabinet on 10th September 2025. Further to this, it should be noted the agreement given by Council in February 2025 for £174million of borrowing is still in place. However, this limit will remain under scrutiny from Cabinet moving forward and subject to decisions as part of the Capital Strategy, not least given the increasing level of regulatory compliance brought in by central government and the Council's current financial situation.

findings.paper_title: 20260909 Appendix D Economic Background and Borrowing Update
findings.headline: Council took £35m temporary borrowing from other local authorities in Q1 requiring replacement and further borrowing during 2026/27
findings.detail: The council borrowed £35m from other local authorities in the first quarter of 2026/27. These loans will mature during the remainder of the financial year. The council anticipates these temporary loans will need to be replaced along with further borrowing required during 2026/27. The council is actively monitoring PWLB rates with the aim of securing longer-term borrowing when rates reduce.
findings.matters: A lender would need to track the council's near-term refinancing requirements, with material short-term borrowing maturing during the year and additional borrowing planned
findings.figures: £35m temporary borrowing
findings.quote: During the first quarter of 2026/27, the Council has taken out temporary borrowing from other local authorities to the value of £35m. These loans will mature during the remainder of 2026/27, and it is anticipated that these will need to be replaced along with further borrowing required during 2026/27.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: UPDATED Financial Monitoring Report Quarter 1 2026.27-02072026 1235 v8
findings.headline: External audit issued statutory recommendations on value-for-money; Council under Non-Statutory Best Value Notice with formal MHCLG reviews beginning September 2026
findings.detail: The 2024/25 external audit 'felt bound to issue statutory recommendations as part of their annual audit... which cast doubt on the integrity of the Council's value for money arrangements'. The Council has been issued a Non-Statutory Best Value Notice requiring regular MHCLG review beginning in September. The council also notes 'Limited Assurance on the Internal Audit Control Framework for seven years'.
findings.matters: Audit concerns, formal Best Value Notice, and active MHCLG oversight indicate external constraint. Governance and financial control weaknesses are matters lenders typically care about.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: UPDATED Financial Monitoring Report Quarter 1 2026.27-02072026 1235 v8
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support reduced to £90m from £121m MTFP forecast, assuming full delivery of favorable in-year variance
findings.detail: The council originally budgeted £121.718m in EFS. Q1 forecast reduces it to £90m. This reduction assumes the £2.291m favorable variance holds and no further pressures emerge. MHCLG is now 'seeking evidence of improvement against their report recommendations and of progressive reductions in the Council's requirements for EFS' as part of active oversight.
findings.matters: While the reduction is welcome, it depends entirely on holding the favorable variance for 8.5 more months. Any adverse movement (worse children's costs, DSG slippage) will push EFS back up. External MHCLG oversight is now active.
findings.figures: Original: £121.718m; Q1 forecast: £90m; reduction £31m
findings.quote: reduced call for EFS in 2026/27 to £90m from the £121m set out in the MTFP report to Council in February 2026, the reduction being in line with the revised MTFP received by Cabinet in July 2026.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: UPDATED Financial Monitoring Report Quarter 1 2026.27-02072026 1235 v8
findings.headline: General Fund Balance remains at £17.291m projected year-end, still short of the £45.815m assessed as needed
findings.detail: GFB was £5m at 1 April 2026 and projects to £17.291m by year-end. However, the council's own Adequacy of Reserves assessment concluded it needs £45.815m. The council is deferring reserve building and banking on four years of favorable variances to reach £35m by 2028/29, 'subject to delivery of the in-year budget'.
findings.matters: At £17.291m, reserves cover only 3.5% of the £489m budget, well below the 5-10% benchmark. Any future adverse variance will force emergency borrowing or EFS calls.
findings.figures: Projected GFB £17.291m; assessed need £45.815m; target £35m by 2028/29
findings.quote: In the Adequacy of Reserves assessment within the Financial Strategy approved by Council in February 2026, the Council identified the need to hold a risk assessed level of £45.815m within the General Fund Balance.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: UPDATED Financial Monitoring Report Quarter 1 2026.27-02072026 1235 v8
findings.headline: Capital programme relies on £39.9m of asset disposals over three years that have not yet been identified
findings.detail: General Fund capital receipts show shortfalls of £19.863m (2027/28), £30.408m (2028/29), and £39.916m (2029/30). The paper notes that 'assets currently being considered for disposal total £41.553m which if realised will still fall short' and acknowledges 'considerable work is required to realise these receipts, with generally a lead in time of at least 12 to 18 months on larger disposals'.
findings.matters: The council has built a three-year capital programme that depends on asset sales lacking identified buyers or timescales. Disposals slip, the council either defers schemes or borrows at prudential rates, increasing debt service costs.
findings.quote: Assets currently being considered for disposal total £41.553m which if realised will still fall short of the total capital receipts required within the capital programme. IT is therefore necessary for the asset base to be reviewed in detail to identify further assets that can be considered for disposal.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant carrying a £46.283m cumulative deficit, managed only via statutory override until March 2028
findings.detail: The DSG is £40.727m in deficit in-year, which produces a cumulative projected deficit of £46.283m. This is managed via a 'Statutory Override agreed nationally by government for DSG deficits through to March 2028'. When the override expires, the council will need to fund the accumulated deficit.
findings.matters: A £46m contingent liability that is only deferred, not resolved, until 2028. When the override expires, the council will need to fund it from General Fund or borrowing.
findings.figures: £40.727m in-year deficit; £46.283m cumulative deficit; override expires March 2028
findings.quote: the overall 2026-27 outturn against centrally retained DSG is forecast to be £40.727m in deficit... This figure is currently managed through a Statutory Override agreed nationally by government for DSG deficits through to March 2028.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: UPDATED Financial Monitoring Report Quarter 1 2026.27-02072026 1235 v8
findings.headline: Children's social care is £3.285m over budget after £2m of unbudgeted pressures emerged post-budget-setting
findings.detail: The £44m children's care budget is projecting a £3.285m overspend. The paper notes that £2m of this overspend arose from 'unbudgeted pressures that were identified over and above what had been included in the 2026/27 budget and after the budget had been set, due to the significant review work required with this budget'. The driver is a sufficiency deficit in foster placements leading to reliance on expensive external residential placements.
findings.matters: A £3.285m overspend in social care (7.5% of that directorate's budget) after just one quarter, with £2m only discovered post-budget, signals planning visibility issues or demand volatility that lenders need to understand.
findings.figures: £3.285m overspend on £44m budget; £2m emerged post-budget-set
findings.quote: the budget for the care of children is £44 million but projecting an overspend of £3.285m. The single largest contributing factor is the increase in External Residential placements and related costs. The increase is directly related to a sufficiency deficit in foster placements, especially for younger children with more complex needs.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit of £46.283m managed through statutory override until March 2028
findings.detail: The council faces an in-year DSG deficit of £40.727m, creating a cumulative deficit of £46.283m (after assumption of 90% write-off via High Needs Stability Grant). This is managed through a national statutory override through March 2028. Three budget pressure areas drive the deficit: top-up funding to mainstream schools and SEND hubs, increased state-funded special school funding, and growth in independent provider placements, totaling £34.843m.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit reflects chronic underfunding of high-needs provision relative to demand growth. While the statutory override provides a short-term safety valve, the deficit must be addressed by March 2028, potentially creating a sudden call on General Fund reserves or requiring service reductions if MHCLG does not extend the override.
findings.figures: In-year DSG deficit: £40.727m; cumulative deficit: £46.283m (after 90% write-off); High Needs Stability Grant: £41.090m; override in place through 31 March 2028; three pressure areas: £34.843m
findings.quote: The overall 2026-27 outturn against centrally retained DSG is forecast to be £40.727m in deficit as at the end of June 2026... overall forecast cumulative DSG deficit position of £46.283m.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Non-Statutory Best Value Notice and MHCLG reviews beginning September 2026; ongoing risk of government intervention if EFS reduction strategy not credible
findings.detail: The council issued a Non-Statutory Best Value Notice requiring regular MHCLG review, with first reviews beginning September 2026. The council's risk register explicitly flags an ongoing risk of government intervention 'including the appointment of envoys or commissioners, should the Council be unable to provide assurance that it has a credible strategy to reduce its reliance on EFS'. The council states it is 'very aware of this risk and would wish to retain control of its own decisions'.
findings.matters: Government intervention through appointment of envoys or commissioners would substantially reduce management autonomy and could trigger operational restructuring. For a lender, intervention risk signals heightened execution risk and potential changes to financial management and strategic decision-making.
findings.figures: MHCLG reviews commence September 2026; statutory override on DSG extends through March 2028; external scrutiny includes CIPFA review (completed May 2026) and Corporate Peer Challenge
findings.quote: There remains an ongoing risk of Government intervention, including the appointment of envoys or commissioners, should the Council be unable to provide assurance that it has a credible strategy to reduce its reliance on EFS and achieve financial sustainability.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: £15m transformation budget deployed at only 20.8% (£3.127m committed); £11.9m assumed to be spent but described as 'likely to move downward'
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes £15m for service transformation to reduce EFS reliance. As of Q1, the Budget, Transformation and Change Panel has approved only £3.127m (20.8%). The council's forecast 'assumes at this time that all transformation funding available through EFS will be consumed although this assumption is likely to move downward as the year progresses'. Unspent transformation funding directly reduces the EFS requirement.
findings.matters: If only £3m of the £15m is actually deployed, the council has materially overstated transformation benefits in its financial recovery projections. Any shortfall would require either additional EFS or further expenditure cuts, undermining the credibility of the Medium-Term Financial Plan.
findings.figures: £15m transformation budget; £3.127m committed (20.8%); £11.9m assumed consumption; each £1m unspent reduces EFS requirement by £1m
findings.quote: This report assumes at this time that all transformation funding available through EFS will be consumed although this assumption is likely to move downward as the year progresses.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Seven years of Limited Assurance from internal audit and statutory recommendations from external auditor on value for money
findings.detail: The council has received Limited Assurance on its internal audit control framework for seven consecutive years. Additionally, the external auditor issued statutory recommendations as part of the 2024/25 audit doubting the council's value for money arrangements. The council acknowledges that recommendations 'require extensive and ongoing work', indicating structural governance deficiencies.
findings.matters: Long-standing audit weaknesses and external auditor statutory recommendations signal structural control and governance issues. This is material to a lender's assessment of management capability, the reliability of council financial data, and the credibility of internal controls over financial reporting.
findings.figures: Seven consecutive years of Limited Assurance; statutory recommendations issued for 2024/25 audit
findings.quote: The Council has reported Limited Assurance on the Internal Audit Control Framework for seven years, limiting confidence in the standards of governance in place within the organisation.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital receipts shortfalls in future years: £19.9m (2027/28), £30.4m (2028/29), £39.9m (2029/30) requiring additional borrowing
findings.detail: The capital programme is heavily reliant on capital receipts for financing. The council projects cumulative shortfalls of £19.863m (2027/28), £30.408m (2028/29), and £39.916m (2029/30). Assets currently considered for disposal total £41.553m, which the council acknowledges will 'still fall short of the total capital receipts required'. Larger disposals typically require 12–18 months lead time.
findings.matters: These shortfalls will be financed by prudential borrowing, adding to the council's debt service costs and interest burden at a time when it is already heavily dependent on EFS. This increases the long-term cost of the capital programme and the council's debt ceiling pressure.
findings.figures: 2027/28: £19.863m shortfall; 2028/29: £30.408m shortfall; 2029/30: £39.916m shortfall; cumulative unmet requirement: assets for disposal £41.553m insufficient; 2026/27 shows surplus of £16.161m
findings.quote: The current capital programme is heavily reliant on the Council generating capital receipts to finance the capital programme. There is a high level of risk in these projections as they are subject to changes in property and land values, the actions of potential buyers and being granted planning permission on sites.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Savings shortfall of £523k with only 90.92% of £5.7m target forecast to be delivered by year-end
findings.detail: The council increased its savings target to £5.7m during Q1 but forecasts delivery of only £5.238m. Specific unachieved savings include: CW002 (CHC income, £375k not yet confirmed), CC003 (Libraries, £112k), CC005 (Museums cost review, £50k), and LG001 (memorial income, £40k). The council states these will be 'delivered in full by the end of the financial year', but several remain unresolved with proposals still being worked through.
findings.matters: Shortfalls in savings require either expenditure cuts elsewhere or increased use of reserves/EFS. This directly impacts the council's ability to demonstrate financial recovery and reduced EFS dependency to MHCLG.
findings.figures: Savings target: £5.7m; forecast delivery: £5.238m; shortfall: £523k (9.08%); individual unachieved savings: £375k, £112k, £50k, £40k
findings.quote: The budget included a saving target of £5m however during quarter 1 this has been increased to £5.7m due to additional savings identified. As at quarter 1 the savings delivery is reporting an adverse variance of £523k

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: £2m in budget pressures discovered after budget was set, indicating forecasting or planning weaknesses
findings.detail: The council reports that £2m of the £3.285m children's overspend 'arose from unbudgeted pressures that were identified over and above what had been included in the 2026/27 budget and after the budget had been set, due to the significant review work required with this budget'. This suggests the initial budget did not capture the full scope of need, requiring mid-year reforecasting.
findings.matters: Discovery of unbudgeted pressures of this magnitude post-setting undermines confidence in the council's planning and forecasting processes, which is critical for a lender assessing the reliability of the council's multi-year EFS reduction trajectory.
findings.figures: £2m of Q1 overspend, representing mid-year budget reforecasting
findings.quote: £2m of this arose from unbudgeted pressures that were identified over and above what had been included in the 2026/27 budget and after the budget had been set, due to the significant review work required with this budget.

findings.committee: Finance and Improvement Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Children's services overspend of £3.285m on £44m budget, driven by external residential placements due to foster placement shortage
findings.detail: The children's care budget is projecting £3.285m overspend, with the largest factor being increased external residential placements caused by insufficient foster placements for children with complex needs. Critically, £2m of this overspend represents pressures identified after the February budget was set. The council is implementing mitigations including reviewing each child in residential care and a Cabinet proposal on 9 September to increase foster carer recruitment.
findings.matters: The council explicitly flags this as 'the largest risk to the delivery of the Council's budget' for 2026/27. An overspend here directly threatens the council's forecast favorable position and its ability to reduce EFS reliance.
findings.figures: £44m budget with £3.285m overspend; £2m unbudgeted pressures identified post-budget-setting; Q1 activity: 9 children stepped down (£1.403m saving), 4 aged out (£922k), but multiple escalations and new admissions to external residential care
findings.quote: The budget for the care of children is £44 million but projecting an overspend of £3.285m. The single largest contributing factor is the increase in External Residential placements and related costs.

findings.headline: Credible plans required to reduce reliance on exceptional financial support in medium to long term
findings.detail: The audit committee noted that the council is currently reliant on exceptional financial support and that credible and serviceable plans are required to reduce this reliance. This indicates the council is receiving bailout funding and has no clear path to financial independence.

findings.detail: Several key service areas have received unsatisfactory or limited audit assurances. findings.quote: The establishment had been subject to repeated audits of it's income collection and letting arrangements and had consistently failed to implement the agreed actions despite management assurances previously provided to the Committee.

findings.paper_title: 20260625 Audit Committee Annual Assurance Report to Council v2
findings.headline: Risk management and assurance framework is not operating as intended and requires improvement
findings.detail: An internal audit review of risk management assessed the control environment as limited with evidence of non-compliance with key controls. The audit committee resolved that improvements are needed in this area. The framework is not functioning as designed.
findings.matters: A broken risk management framework means the council's risk assessments and reported positions cannot be relied upon for decision-making, including about financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Risk management audit overall assessment: limited; evidence of non-compliance with some key controls

findings.paper_title: 20260625 Audit Committee Annual Assurance Report to Council v2
findings.headline: Loss of key staff through voluntary redundancy programme is placing pressure on improvement and transformation delivery
findings.detail: The council has carried out a voluntary redundancy programme that has resulted in the loss of key officers and the creation of interim roles in statutory positions. The audit committee identified this as placing further pressure on the delivery of required improvement activities and transformation work at a time when governance and control strengthening is critical.
findings.matters: Reducing capacity in the middle of a major governance improvement programme suggests the council is unable to fund improvement work and maintain delivery simultaneously, which undermines confidence in turnaround plans.
findings.figures: Key officers lost through voluntary redundancy; statutory positions filled only by interim arrangements
findings.quote: The loss of key officers through the Council's voluntary redundancy programme, interim roles including those in statutory positions place further pressure on the delivery of the required improvement activities and required transformation works.
