findings.headline: Strategic risks show no improvement over two years; audit committee questions effectiveness of mitigating actions
findings.detail: Members of the audit committee explicitly noted that no strategic risks had improved over the last two years and questioned whether the mitigating actions being taken are actually effective. This indicates that the risk management system is not delivering results.
findings.matters: If mitigating actions are not working and risks are not improving, the council's risk management system is ineffective, meaning reported risk assessments may not reflect the true trajectory of problems.
findings.figures: No risks improved over 2 years
findings.quote: Members noted that no risks had improved over the last two years and questioned the effectiveness of mitigating actions.

findings.paper_title: 20260625 Audit Committee Annual Assurance Report to Council v2
findings.headline: All 10 strategic risks rated above tolerance level, including inability to contain expenditure and set balanced budgets
findings.detail: The strategic risk register shows 10 risks with 9 rated as high risk and 1 as medium. Critically, 100% of these are above the council's tolerance level. Three risks are scored at the maximum level of 25: cyber attack impact, inability to contain expenditure within available resources, and inability to set a balanced budget within the medium-term financial strategy.
findings.matters: An inability to contain expenditure or set balanced budgets within the MTFS indicates the council cannot guarantee financial discipline or budget outcomes, which directly affects repayment capacity.
findings.figures: 10 strategic risks with 100% above tolerance level; 3 risks at maximum score of 25; 9 high risk, 1 medium risk
findings.quote: 100% of strategic risks were above the tolerance level... Three strategic risks were scores at the maximum level of 25, those being: - Failure to protect and manage the impact of a targeted cyber attack on ICT systems used by the Authority. - Inability to contain overall committed expenditure within the current available resources within this financial year. - Inability to set a balanced budget for a given year within the MTFS

findings.paper_title: 20260625 Audit Committee Annual Assurance Report to Council v2
findings.headline: External auditors warned of Section 114 notice risk if financial position does not improve significantly and rapidly
findings.detail: Grant Thornton raised concerns about the council's financial position and indicated that a Section 114 notice (formal intervention requiring the council to set aside money and cease spending) may be needed if the situation does not improve significantly and rapidly. The financial situation was described as 'unprecedented' and has worsened over the past three years from a position already deemed 'perilous'.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a critical formal intervention in councils facing financial distress. This warning indicates substantial default risk and the council may not have funding certainty in the medium term.
findings.figures: Financial situation adjudged perilous 3 years ago and has worsened; unprecedented current financial situation
findings.quote: The Committee received the External Auditor's letter highlighting their concerns about the Council's financial position and the potential need for a Section 114 notice if the position did not improved significantly and rapidly.

findings.paper_title: 20260625 Audit Committee Annual Assurance Report to Council v2
findings.headline: Chief Audit Executive has given limited assurance for seven consecutive years with no improvement
findings.detail: The audit committee has received only limited assurance on the council's governance and control framework for seven years in succession. The committee explicitly states it is concerned that there has been no demonstrable improvement in the internal control environment during 2025/26 despite multiple improvement plans. This represents a sustained governance failure across the entire council.
findings.matters: Seven years without improvement indicates the council's governance framework is not functioning effectively and improvement efforts are not delivering results, which is a critical risk for financial stability and borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: 7 years of limited assurance opinions; no risks improved over the last two years
findings.quote: The Chief Audit Executive's overall opinion on the control environment has been 'Limited' for seven years. The Committee shares the concern that there has been no demonstrable improvement in the internal control environment during 2025/26.

findings.headline: Interim s151 Officer in post; fundamental review of financial governance underway following financial emergency
findings.detail: The document refers to the "Interim s151 Officer" reviewing financial risks (section 5.4), suggesting the chief finance officer position has been vacant or recently changed. Section 5.1 states: "The financial results for 2025/26 confirm the need for a fundamental review of key risks and mitigations for budget preparation, monitoring and control of Council finances." The council acknowledges "work is underway to make improvements to the Council's financial monitoring and budget setting arrangements, learning from lessons of the past".
findings.matters: A change in the s151 officer position during a financial crisis suggests governance instability. The need for fundamental review of budget planning and monitoring indicates previous systems failed to detect or prevent a £49m overspend and £33m in unachieved savings.
findings.figures: Financial emergency declared September 2025; fundamental review underway
findings.quote: These risks and mitigations are currently subject to review by the Interim s151 Officer and will be reported to Cabinet in July as part of the MTFP update. The financial results for 2025/26 confirm the need for a fundamental review of key risks and mitigations for budget preparation, monitoring and control of Council finances.

findings.headline: Multi-year reliance on Exceptional Financial Support; EFS required "for multiple years" until spending matches resources
findings.detail: The document states: "it is recognised that EFS will be required for multiple years until such time that net spending can be reduced to a level that matches resources available". The council also acknowledges that EFS "represents a 'permission' to borrow and the consequential borrowing incurs the cost of financing that debt which needs to be provided for within revenue budget". The MTFP for 2026/27 and beyond will be reviewed, with an updated version due to Cabinet in July 2026.
findings.matters: Multi-year reliance on emergency government funding indicates the council faces structural (not cyclical) financial problems. This creates ongoing debt service obligations from a revenue budget that is already in severe stress, suggesting limited long-term sustainability without major service reductions or income changes.
findings.figures: £61.791m 2025/26 EFS; EFS approved by "approximately 50 other Councils across England" in this round
findings.quote: In making this application, it was recognised that EFS will be required for multiple years until such time that net spending can be reduced to a level that matches resources available. It is recognised, but unfortunate, that EFS represents a 'permission' to borrow and that the consequential borrowing incurs the cost of financing that debt.

findings.headline: North-West Relief Road capital scheme cancelled; £32.154m of EFS used to write off accumulated costs
findings.detail: The council cancelled the NWRR project during 2025/26 "owing to affordability issues". The synopsis explicitly states the EFS was needed to "write back to the General Fund the capital costs of the aborted North West Relief Road project that had become unaffordable". The council had budgeted £39.900m in EFS for NWRR but utilised only £32.154m (the balance going to the Oxon Link Road which remained in the capital programme). This represents a capital investment decision that failed.
findings.matters: A cancelled capital project funded through borrowing raises questions about capital project appraisal, affordability assessment, and governance. The fact it became unaffordable mid-project is a concern for future capital planning credibility.
findings.figures: £39.900m originally budgeted for NWRR in EFS; £32.154m ultimately utilised; project cancelled 26th February 2026
findings.quote: Approximately £39m of the 2025/26 EFS was scheduled to be used the financial consequences of the decision to abort the North-West Relief Road project owing to affordability issues.

findings.headline: Children's external residential placements £14.908m over budget despite 7.5% reduction in looked-after children
findings.detail: Despite reducing the number of children in the council's care from 721 to 667 (a 7.5% reduction), external residential placements overspent by £14.908m. External spot/framework placements were up £9.372m and disabled children's team residential costs up £3.074m due to "increase in numbers". The document notes "a combination of known, but unbudgeted pressures" were the driver. This indicates increasing complexity and cost per child.
findings.matters: Increasing per-capita costs in a reducing population indicates either worsening case severity, poor procurement, or both—all of which are concerning for long-term budget sustainability and suggest the underlying demand is more expensive than anticipated.
findings.figures: £14.908m overspend on external residential placements; looked-after children down 7.5% (721 to 667); spot/framework £9.372m over; disabled children's residential £3.074m over
findings.quote: despite an overall 7.5% reduction of the number of children looked after from 721 on 1st April 2025 to 667 on 31st March 2026, a combination of known, but unbudgeted pressures, aligned with demand led pressures within Children's placements leading to a £14.908m spend over budget on external residential placements.

findings.headline: Adult social care spot purchasing overran budget by £16.140m; nursing and complexity pressures unbudgeted
findings.detail: Care & Wellbeing overspent by £26.397m. Within this, spot purchasing (residential care) was £16.140m over budget. The breakdown shows: residential care demographic demand £9.004m, nursing complexity and cases transferred from health £6.061m, and individual service fund pressures £3.859m. Block purchasing (supported living) added a further £13.327m overspend due to "increase in complexity of care and provider market challenges around capacity and uplifts". These are demand-led pressures that were not forecasted.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled social care demand is the largest and most intractable pressure facing local authorities. If a council cannot forecast or manage demand in this category, it indicates structural financial fragility and long-term sustainability risk.
findings.figures: £26.397m Care & Wellbeing overspend; spot purchasing £16.140m over (residential £9.004m, nursing £6.061m); block purchasing £13.327m over
findings.quote: £21.899m pressure budget purchasing made up of: - £16.140m SPOT Gross purchasing - £9.004m Residential care demographic demand increases to budget set £6.061m increase in nursing due to complexity and cases transferred from health to local authority, £3.859m pressure on Individual Service Funds... - 13.327m BLOCK Gross purchasing pressure on supported living and supported living Individual Service Funds due to an increase in complexity of care.

findings.headline: General Fund Balance depleted to £5.000m—well below appropriate levels for a council this size
findings.detail: The council brought forward £4.825m in reserves and budgeted a £29.455m contribution. However, it drew down £29.278m to cover overspends, leaving only £5m. The council explicitly acknowledges: "the current combination of earmarked and un-earmarked (General) reserves of £34.069m is at a level that is below that would normally seen as appropriate for a Council of this size". Independent guidance suggests reserves should be 5–15% of net spending (£14.4–43.3m).
findings.matters: Depleted reserves eliminate a council's buffer against unexpected shocks, limit its capacity to manage emergencies, and indicate dependence on EFS for normal operations. A £5m buffer against £338m of spend provides virtually no shock absorption.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance £5.000m (year-end); brought forward £4.825m; budgeted contribution £29.455m; actual draw-down £29.278m; total reserves £34.069m
findings.quote: Note the current combination of earmarked and un-earmarked (General) reserves of £34.069m is at a level that is below that would normally seen as appropriate for a Council of this size.

findings.headline: Only 29.6% of savings targets delivered (£17.722m of £59.401m); £33.379m of unachieved savings
findings.detail: The council failed to deliver 70.4% of its planned savings in 2025/26. The document notes these variances "have been reported consistently through to Cabinet during 2025/26" despite management controls. The unachieved savings sit primarily in Corporate Budgets (£33.379m). The MTFP removes most unachieved savings for 2026/27 but replaces them with "a more modest but achievable savings target of at least £5m".
findings.matters: If a council cannot execute its own financial recovery plan and savings programmes, this indicates either weak governance, poor planning capability, or operational inability—all red flags for lenders assessing the council's capacity to manage its affairs.
findings.figures: £17.722m delivered; £59.401m target; 29.6% achievement rate; £33.379m unachieved (70.4%)
findings.quote: only 29.6% of the 2025/26 savings required have been delivered, amounting to £17.722m. The MTFP for 2026/27 and beyond sets out the removal of most of the 70.4% of unachieved savings.

findings.headline: £61.791m Exceptional Financial Support from government—emergency borrowing to balance accounts
findings.detail: The council applied for government bailout funding following a financial emergency declared in September 2025. The council states EFS "enables the Council to borrow funds which will be repaid through increasing the capital financing revenue budget". The final EFS drawdown was £61.791m (£9.609m less than the £71.4m originally approved). The use includes £32.154m to write off the cancelled North-West Relief Road capital scheme.
findings.matters: A lender views emergency government support as a marker of insolvency. The council could not balance its books through normal means and required state intervention. This creates future debt repayment obligations funded from revenue.
findings.figures: £61.791m EFS utilised (vs. £71.4m approved); ~50 other councils across England submitted EFS applications in 2025/26
findings.quote: it was necessary for the Council to make an application to the Government for EFS to ensure that sufficient resources were available to balance the financial position in 2025/26. EFS is the government's preferred route for supporting Councils in financial difficulty.

findings.headline: £49.428m revenue overspend (17% above budget) driven by unachieved savings and unrecognised demand pressures
findings.detail: The council budgeted £288.586m but spent £338.014m. The synopsis directly states the overspend resulted from "ambitious savings targets" that proved unachievable and "failure to recognise embedded demand pressures across social care". Care & Wellbeing overspent by £26.397m and Children & Young People by £12.230m.
findings.matters: A lender assesses a council's ability to forecast and control spending. A 17% overspend indicates either severe planning failures or inability to manage in-year pressures—both are critical solvency risks.
findings.figures: £49.428m adverse variation; budget £288.586m, outturn £338.014m
findings.quote: The net adverse variation to the budget for the year amounted to £49.428m. This was directly and for a major part a consequence of a budget having been set that included ambitious savings targets and the failure to recognise embedded demand pressures across social care which proved to be unachievable.

findings.paper_title: REPORT Update on the Children's Services Reforms.docx Final
findings.headline: Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) timeliness significantly below benchmark at 36.5%, with rising demand placing additional assessment pressure
findings.detail: Shropshire's statutory timeliness for issuing EHCPs is 36.5% of new plans within the required 20 weeks (excluding exceptions), compared to neighbour average of 50.2% and England average of 46.4%. Additionally, the number of families requesting EHCPs has risen substantially since national reforms were announced, placing further pressure on assessment capacity. This is a statutory compliance issue.
findings.matters: Below-benchmark statutory performance indicates the council is struggling to meet legal obligations in a high-demand area. Combined with rising request volumes, this signals system stress and heightens risk of audit findings, regulatory intervention, or reputational damage.
findings.figures: 36.5% of EHCPs issued within 20 weeks (2024, excluding exceptions); 50.2% neighbour average; 46.4% England average; Statutory deadline 20 weeks; Rising demand for EHCPs reported
findings.quote: Statutory timeliness for the delivery of our education health and care plans is below benchmark: 36.5% of new EHCPs issued within 20 weeks (excluding exceptions) in 2024 vs neighbours (50.2%) and England (46.4%).

findings.paper_title: REPORT Update on the Children's Services Reforms.docx Final
findings.headline: Grant funding increases from £2.039m (2025/26) to £5.872m (2027/28) but is time-limited and ringfenced; uncertainty beyond 2029
findings.detail: Funding for Children, Families and Youth programmes is being consolidated from multiple grants. Total funding rises to £5.872m by 2027/28 (Families First £2.872m, Best Start in Life £1.057m, SEND £1.943m) from £2.039m in 2025/26. However, grants are ringfenced to specific activities with restricted use, and "there is a risk that the short term funding is not extended beyond 2029." The DfE investment assumes nationally identified demographic factors, not Shropshire's actual demand.
findings.matters: The transformation plan is substantially enabled by time-limited government grants with uncertain continuation. If grants are not extended or reduced, the council will need to either absorb preventative service investment into base budgets or reduce programme scope. This creates contingent funding risk.
findings.figures: £2.039m total grants (2025/26); £5.872m total grants (2027/28); £2.872m Families First Partnership (2027/28); £1.057m Best Start in Life (2027/28); £1.943m SEND (2027/28, indicative); funding growth £3.833m in two years
findings.quote: There is a risk that the short term funding is not extended beyond 2029... The investment we have received from the DfE is based on nationally identified demographic factors for Shropshire not actual demand in Shropshire. This means that the investment is not sufficient to reform the system, whilst meeting the current service demand in the system.

findings.paper_title: REPORT Update on the Children's Services Reforms.docx Final
findings.headline: Financial model contains 25 explicit assumptions with risks including that care reductions will translate to cost savings—evidence suggests they may not
findings.detail: The model acknowledges that a 5% reduction in children in care numbers (September 2025 to May 2026) has not yet yielded a 5% cost reduction. The model's assumptions include that outcomes will match pathfinder areas (which may not reflect Shropshire's rurality and market context), that placement market volatility will not spike costs, that practice change will be sustained, and that partners will maintain contribution. The report explicitly notes all assumptions require "close monitoring, review and agile adjustment."
findings.matters: The savings plan underpins the council's financial sustainability narrative. If key assumptions fail (e.g., foster care market does not expand, partner contributions lapse, practice change does not embed), the savings timeline slips and the council carries investment cost for longer without relief.
findings.figures: 5% reduction in children in care (Sept 2025-May 2026) with no proportional cost reduction observed; Model assumes 9% average reduction in all care types combined; Return on investment assumed at 3 years; Cumulative impact deficit in 2028/29 under realistic scenario (£4.142m)
findings.quote: Reductions in Children Looked After numbers does not automatically translate into a similar reduction in cost or overall spend (eg Children in Care number have reduced by 5% between September 2025 and May 2026, but we have not seen a 5% reduction in costs)... All these assumptions mean that the implementation of the programme needs close monitoring, review and agile adjustment.

findings.paper_title: REPORT Update on the Children's Services Reforms.docx Final
findings.headline: Transformation plan requires £2m investment from 2027/28 with savings not projected until 2029/30; full payback of initial £2m investment not until 2031/32
findings.detail: The council plans investment of £2m per annum from 2027/28 (with £0.9m in 2028/29) to fund prevention and rebalance services. Best case savings reach £11.418m cumulatively by 2032/33, but realistic case projects only £8.326m. The 4-year lag before material savings appears means the council must absorb investment costs while waiting for demand reduction. Modelled savings assume 9% reduction in children in care numbers.
findings.matters: This is an invest-to-save model with extended payoff horizon. The council must front-load significant investment before reductions materialise. Success depends on sustained practice change, achieving 9% care reduction, partner engagement, and placement market improvements—all of which carry execution risk.
findings.figures: £2.000m investment (2027/28); £0.900m investment (2028/29); £1.483m savings (2029/30); £3.709m savings (2030/31); Best case cumulative savings £11.418m (to 2032/33); Realistic case cumulative savings £8.326m (to 2032/33); Payback 2031/32
findings.quote: It is estimated that investment in staff and systems will be approximately £2 million per annum with effect from 2027/28... Current estimates suggest that the MTFP can project savings in the Children's Services budget of £1.483m in 2029/30 rising to a further £3.709m in 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: REPORT Update on the Children's Services Reforms.docx Final
findings.headline: Children in care rate of 111 per 10,000 is 81% above statistical neighbours and 65% above England; 80% of children's budget spent on social care vs 47% national average
findings.detail: Shropshire has 111 children in care per 10,000 population (May 2026), compared to neighbour mean of 61 and England of 67.1. Critically, the council spends circa 80% of its children's services budget on social care placements versus the national average of 47%, with only 20% available for prevention. Additionally, 15% of placements are in secure homes and children's homes versus neighbours at 12.6%.
findings.matters: This structural imbalance is the defining sustainability issue. The council is spending significantly more than demographic factors justify, and the heavy reliance on expensive residential placements makes the budget unaffordable without rebalancing. This cannot be managed within normal budget flexibility.
findings.figures: 111 per 10,000 children in care (May 2026); 61 per 10,000 neighbour mean; 67.1 per 10,000 England average; 80% of children's budget on social care vs 47% national average; 15% of placements in secure/residential homes (vs neighbours 12.6%)
findings.quote: The Children in Care rate remains the defining sustainability issue: 111 per 10,000 (May 2026), well above the neighbour mean (61) and England ￼comparator (67.1)... in Shropshire we spend circa 80% of every pound on Children's Social Care whereas the average is 47% spent on Children's Social Care and 53% on preventative services.

findings.paper_title: REPORT Update on the Children's Services Reforms.docx Final
findings.headline: Children's placements budget overspent by £14.908m in 2025/26, with growth budget of £19.342m added to 2026/27 to address forward pressures
findings.detail: External residential placements exceeded budget by £14.908m in 2025/26 due to increased numbers. The council has added £19.342m growth to the 2026/27 placements budget to manage forecast demand. Overall Children and Young People's services overspent by £12.230m against a budget of £90.963m. This is a demand-led budget line with limited controllability in-year.
findings.matters: Placement costs are volatile and demand-driven. The large growth allocation signals the council expects continued pressure. If demand does not moderate as the transformation programme projects, the council will face additional significant overspends beyond the budgeted growth.
findings.figures: £14.908m overspend on External Residential placements (2025/26); £19.342m growth budget (2026/27); £12.230m total Children and Young People's overspend (2025/26); £44m total placement budget (2026/27)
findings.quote: a £14.908m overspend on External Residential placements within the Children's placements budget where numbers had increased significantly in year. Growth of £19.342m has been built into the 2026/27 Children's External Residential placements budget to address this budget pressure going forward.

findings.paper_title: REPORT Update on the Children's Services Reforms.docx Final
findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block deficit of £45.655m, partially cleared by 90% grant but leaving £4.565m exposure for 2026/27 onwards
findings.detail: Shropshire's cumulative DSG deficit reached £45.655m by end of 2025/26, with the 2025/26 in-year deficit alone at £28.090m. The council is eligible for a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the historic deficit (approximately £41m), but this leaves a £4.565m deficit position for 2026/27 onwards. The DfE has signalled willingness to support future in-year deficits through appropriate measures, but "it will not be unlimited."
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this scale represents a material liability. The grant dependency for 90% relief means future support is uncertain beyond current commitments, and ongoing in-year deficits are expected as SEND reforms embed.
findings.figures: £45.655m cumulative deficit (to end 2025/26); £28.090m in-year deficit (2025/26); £41m High Needs Stability Grant (90%); £4.565m remaining deficit (2026/27 onwards)
findings.quote: Shropshire's cumulative DSG deficit is £45.655m up to the end of the 2025/26 financial year... In Shropshire the 90% High Needs Stability Grant is worth c.£41m, leaving the Council to fund the remaining 10%.

findings.headline: Schools capital £11.17m in 2026/27, £26.94m in 2027/28, £2.5m in 2028/29; Phase 4 funding of £24.5m all in 2027/28
findings.detail: Schools Future Place Planning Phase 4 allocation of £24.5m appears only in 2027/28 (zero in 2026/27 and 2029/30), funded entirely by DfE Basic Need Grant. Includes expansions at 9 secondary schools (Belvidere 6 classrooms, Meole Brace dining, St Giles, Moreton Say, Lakelands, Corbet, Mary Webb, Ludlow, Whitchurch) plus Ironbridge new school. Total schools capital rises from £11.2m (2026/27) to £26.9m (2027/28), then falls to £2.5m (2028/29).
findings.matters: Concentration of £26.9m schools capital in one year signals anticipated place pressure and requires sustained delivery capacity. A lender must assess whether the council can manage this capital surge while maintaining other capital programmes and operational services.

findings.detail: The Major Repairs Programme for Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund shows £4.433m prudential borrowing in 2026/27 alongside £2.237m DESNZ grant. findings.detail: Swimming in Shropshire (£200k), Pride Hill Shopping Centre Regeneration (£500k), and Commercial Investments Unallocated (£225.9k) are all proposed to be paused and budgets removed. These were previously budgeted schemes now being withdrawn from the capital programme.
findings.matters: Pausing previously-committed capital schemes signals either financial constraint, changed priorities, or cash flow pressure. A lender needs to understand whether these reflect temporary market adjustments or more fundamental financial challenges.

findings.headline: £10m annual efficiency savings planned with 45–58% risk of non-achievement from 2027/28 onwards

This creates annual risk-adjusted impacts of £4,555k–£5,856k and indicates significant uncertainty about whether these savings will materialize.

findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) SEND deficit climbs from £42,089k in 2026/27 to £92,089k by 2028/29. From 2028/29 onwards, the council risk-assesses this at 15–25%, with the planned deficit then dropping to £25,000k in 2029/30, suggesting either government intervention or a policy shift to manage the liability.
findings.matters: SEND deficits represent statutory education obligations that fall to the local authority if DSG funding is insufficient; growing deficits force either service reductions or require council reserves to absorb the shortfall
findings.figures: DSG-SEND Deficit of £42,089k (2026/27), growing to £67,089k (2027/28) and £92,089k (2028/29), with risk-assessed value of £13,813k (2028/29); reduces to £25,000k (2029/30) with £6,250k risk-assessed

findings.headline: Pension triennial valuation unaffordable, with growing costs from £99.6m to £112.1m over five years
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies 'Pension triennial valuation unaffordable' in its risk assessment. findings.figures: Pension cost budget of £99,637k (2026/27) rising to £112,142k (2030/31); risk-assessed values of £0 through 2028/29, then £3,266k (2029/30) and £3,364k (2030/31)

findings.detail: The council had committed to efficiency savings across all service areas—including Care & Wellbeing (adult social care redesign, nighttime care, telecare), Children & Young People (rightsizing, agency staff reduction), Corporate functions (third party spend, rightsizing, income generation), and Enabling services (property rationalization, new operating model). These savings are now marked as unachievable and growth funding is being allocated instead to preserve services at current run rates.

findings.headline: High Needs (SEND education) deficit of £42.089m will force further budget cuts
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant for high needs education carries a deficit of £42.089m by end of March 2026. findings.paper_title: 20260226Council - Draft 2026.27 General Fund budgets and MTFP
findings.headline: Previously approved savings have not been achieved and are being added back as new growth
findings.detail: The council has reversed unachieved savings from prior years, which now sit on the 2026/27 base budget as new growth to be offset. This directly signals that the council's prior transformation and cost-reduction programmes have failed to deliver, creating execution risk on its new Financial Sustainability Strategy.

findings.paper_title: 20260226Council - Draft 2026.27 General Fund budgets and MTFP
findings.headline: Council tax has been raised to the absolute maximum allowable to fund the deficit
findings.detail: The council is proposing an 8.99% council tax rise (6.99% general increase plus 2% adult social care precept), utilising full flexibility granted by central government. The band D rate reaches £1,969.09. This is the maximum the council is permitted to raise without a referendum, and the council is using all of it.
findings.matters: This signals financial desperation. When a council moves to maximum allowable taxation, it indicates it has exhausted discretionary revenue measures and is now dependent entirely on statutory limits and government support.
findings.figures: 8.99% council tax rise; Band D rate of £1,969.09; additional income from 4% flexibility: £8.8m
findings.quote: proposes to fully utilise the permitted council tax flexibility and accordingly, the level of EFS necessary is proposed to be reduced to £121m. An increase in council tax of 8.99% would result in additional income of £8.8m for 2026/27

findings.paper_title: 20260226Council - Draft 2026.27 General Fund budgets and MTFP
findings.headline: General Fund balance without Emergency Financial Support would be negative £16.465m; with support projected at only £5.001m, requiring £42.676m contribution in 2026/27
findings.detail: Without EFS, the council's General Fund balance would be negative £16.465m at 31 March 2026, an unsustainable position. Even with the requested EFS, balances will be only £5.001m, which the council itself judges insufficient for the risks it faces. The council is rebuilding through a planned contribution of £42.676m in 2026/27, meaning reserves are being entirely driven by government support, not accumulated from operations.
findings.matters: Reserves are a lender's first line of security for covenant compliance. The fact they have collapsed to near-zero and can only be restored through exceptional government grants is a critical weakness.
findings.figures: Balance as at 1 April 2025: £4,825k; projected without EFS: (£16,465k); planned balance 31 March 2026 with EFS: £5,001k; required contribution 2026/27: £42.676m
findings.quote: the deteriorating financial position of the council has reduced the General Fund Balance to an unsustainable level and has left the Council with no substantial reserves on which to fall back on should any emergency occur.

findings.paper_title: 20260226Council - Draft 2026.27 General Fund budgets and MTFP
findings.headline: Council cannot balance its budget without £121m in government-backed borrowing
findings.detail: The council requires £121m in Exceptional Financial Support to set a legally balanced budget for 2026/27. This borrowing is not a one-off: the council also required £71.4m for 2025/26 and faces ongoing shortfalls across the medium term. The council notes that borrowing to balance revenue budgets is uncommon but that an increasing number of councils are resorting to it.
findings.matters: This is a fundamental solvency question for any lender. It means the council cannot meet its obligations from revenue sources and is dependent on continued government approval of exceptional support applications.
findings.figures: £121m EFS for 2026/27 (down from £130m), £71.4m for 2025/26, gross expenditure of £922.853m
findings.quote: utilising borrowing to balance revenue budgets is not common across the sector, although an increasing number of councils are finding it necessary to take this course of action. EFS is not intended as a long-term solution, nor is it sustainable

findings.headline: Seasonal cash flow pressure in February and March creates liquidity vulnerability
findings.detail: The strategy identifies that council tax collection drops in February and March, causing cash balances to fall during these months. The council mitigates by holding cash in call accounts rather than fixed-term investments, but the vulnerability is explicitly acknowledged as a risk to meeting investment benchmarks.
findings.matters: Predictable seasonal cash crunches could delay service payments or borrowing repayments if the council's financial position deteriorates further.
findings.figures: None quantified; seasonal pattern in Feb–March collection noted
findings.quote: Also during the months of February and March the Council does not collect as much Council Tax and so cash balances reduce during these months in particular.

findings.headline: Reserves and cash balances have reduced significantly, constraining liquidity
findings.detail: The risk table explicitly flags that 'reserves and hence cash balances have reduced' as a key constraint on the council's ability to invest cash and manage cash flow. Investment benchmarks are also at risk, particularly in February and March when council tax collection is lower and cash balances are weakest.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves mean the council has less buffer for unexpected demands or revenue shortfalls and may struggle to meet obligations if cash flow deteriorates further.
findings.figures: £24.2m investments held as at 31 December 2025
findings.quote: The availability of cash for investing has also become a key factor, especially in a period where reserves and hence cash balances have reduced.

findings.headline: Additional borrowing approved and sought, including assumed Exceptional Financial Support from government
findings.detail: The council plans prudential borrowing of £59m over 2026/27–2028/29, plus a further £17.6m for future prioritised schemes through 2030/31. Critically, the strategy includes 'borrowing as a result of assumed approval of Exceptional Financial Support', suggesting the council is seeking or expecting government bailout funding.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support signals DLUHC has identified the council as unable to balance its budget normally; it is discretionary and can be withdrawn or limited. Additional borrowing on top of £415m existing debt raises refinance and liquidity risk.
findings.figures: £59m prudential borrowing (2026/27–2028/29), £17.6m further schemes (2026/27–2030/31), existing debt £415m (£383m PWLB)
findings.quote: Currently the approved borrowing requirement identified within the approved Capital Programme 2026/27 to 2028/29 is prudential borrowing of £59m. In addition to this there is an anticipated prudential borrowing requirement for future prioritised schemes in the Capital Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31 of £17.6m and borrowing as a result of assumed approval of Exceptional Financial Support.

findings.headline: Financial emergency declared, driving unprecedented management action
findings.detail: Cabinet declared a financial emergency on 10 September 2025 due to unprecedented financial demands. All non-essential spend is to be stopped and essential spend challenged, with actions including scaling down initiatives, changing activity scope, and delaying or extending plans. The council is managing this through all levels of the organization.
findings.matters: A declared financial emergency is a material credit event and signals the council is in acute distress, requiring lenders to reassess risk and repayment capacity.
findings.figures: Financial emergency declared 10 September 2025
findings.quote: Shropshire Council continues to manage unprecedented financial demands and a financial emergency was declared by Cabinet on 10 September 2025.

findings.headline: Voluntary redundancy and transformation costs of £26.008m in capital receipts required in 2025/26; if capital receipts targets are missed, further revenue pressure emerges
findings.detail: The council is depending on £26.008m of capital receipts to fund transformation activities: £10.863m for VRP (voluntary redundancies, with £3.468m more needed in 2025/26), £0.226m compulsory redundancies, £7.844m transformation projects, and £7.075m for Strategic Transformation Partner costs. The report notes that 'Delays in realisation of capital receipts in 2025/26, suggest a potential shortfall during the year'. If capital receipt targets are not met, either (a) transformation activity must be funded from revenue (worsening the deficit), or (b) capital receipts will be insufficient to cover redundancy costs, creating unfunded people costs.
findings.matters: A council that is paying out significant redundancy costs while trying to save money is in a vulnerable position. If asset sales don't materialize as planned, the authority could face both redundancy liabilities and inability to fund transformation, creating a double squeeze.
findings.figures: Capital receipts requirement for transformation £26.008m (VRP £10.863m, compulsory £0.226m, projects £7.844m, STP £7.075m); Central scenario assumes £10.0m capital receipts in Q4; Adverse scenario assumes £10.0m shortfall vs budget
findings.quote: Delays in realisation of capital receipts in 2025/26, suggest a potential shortfall during the year, available to fund transformation activities.

findings.headline: Interest payable pressures of £3.190m suggest borrowing costs are rising faster than forecast, with significant new borrowing being drawn for capital and revenue needs
findings.detail: Corporate budgets show a £3.190m pressure 'against interest payable relating to borrowing costs'. This is not explained in detail but in context of a £155m potential borrowing requirement for NWRR and overall revenue deficit funding needs, it indicates treasury costs are tracking above assumptions. The council has engaged treasury advisors (MUFG) and is maintaining a £20m cash buffer with borrowing anticipated for 2025/26 'built into the P7 monitoring position'. However, if the NWRR is cancelled or if EFS is late or reduced, additional unbudgeted borrowing may be required.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs without corresponding revenue growth tightens the budget further. Additional borrowing (whether for NWRR completion or to cover the deficit) will increase the revenue budget pressure in future years through MRP and interest. This creates a ratchet effect where each year starts with higher committed costs.
findings.figures: Interest payable pressure £3.190m; MUFG treasury advisors engaged; £20m cash buffer maintained; Borrowing requirement for 2025/26 built into monitoring
findings.quote: £3.190m pressures against interest payable relating to borrowing costs

findings.headline: Authority is entirely dependent on securing £71.4m Exceptional Financial Support from government; without it, a Section 114 report would be required
findings.detail: The council has applied for £71.4m in Exceptional Financial Support, comprised of £22.4m for revenue, £10.0m for transformation unable to be funded from capital receipts, and £39.0m for potential NWRR write-off. The report states: 'Confirmation of Exceptional Financial Support to the value of £71.4m, alongside the establishment of a contingency reserve of £5.478m and a proposed year end balance of £5m will ensure that the central, favourable and adverse scenarios can be accommodated would remove the need for a section 114 Report to be issued.' This is 'underpinned by legal advice from a leading barrister in this area.' There is no contingency if the application is refused or reduced.
findings.matters: A Section 114 report is issued when a council cannot balance its budget and is in effect insolvent. EFS is discretionary government support, not guaranteed. If refused or reduced, the authority's financial position would be legally untenable. Lenders cannot rely on discretionary government grants that may not materialize.
findings.figures: EFS application £71.4m (£22.4m revenue + £10.0m transformation + £39.0m NWRR); Without EFS, projected General Fund Balance is £16.465m negative; With EFS, projected year-end balance £5.001m
findings.quote: Confirmation of Exceptional Financial Support to the value of £71.4m, alongside the establishment of a contingency reserve of £5.478m and a proposed year end balance of £5m will ensure that the central, favourable and adverse scenarios can be accommodated would remove the need for a section 114 Report to be issued. This assessment is underpinned by legal advice from a leading barrister in this area.

findings.headline: North West Relief Road project paused with £38.895m sunk cost; central scenario assumes £13.495m write-off via Capitalization Direction, adverse scenario £38.895m total write-off
findings.detail: The NWRR project is paused 'pending review in light of increasing borrowing requirement of £155m'. The authority has spent £38.895m to date. In the central forecast scenario, £20.4m DfT LLMF funding, £4.2m LEP funding, and £0.8m other funding are retained, but the balance of £13.495m would need a Capitalization Direction (funded from EFS borrowing) to write off to revenue. In the adverse scenario, all three funding sources are clawed back and the entire £38.895m requires capitalization direction write-off. This is included in the council's £71.4m EFS application (£39.0m specifically for 'revenue costs arising from the need to write off' the scheme if cancelled).
findings.matters: A £155m borrowing requirement for a now-paused capital project is a red flag for capital governance and project appraisal. The authority has already spent £39m and faces between £13.5m and £39m additional revenue cost depending on funding clawback decisions outside its control. This is a live material risk that could deteriorate further.
findings.figures: NWRR spend to date £38.895m; Borrowing requirement for project £155m; Central scenario write-off requirement £13.495m; Adverse scenario write-off requirement £38.895m (total); EFS application includes £39.0m for NWRR write-off
findings.quote: Decision taken to pause NWRR. If Council decide to cancel the scheme, spend to date of £38.895m needs to be accounted for. Central assumption: £20.4m DfT LLMF retained. £4.2m LEP funding for OLR retained. £0.8m other OLR spend retained. Balance £13.495m would need a Capitalisation Direction through EFS to enable write off to revenue funded from borrowing.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit has grown to £42.089m, locked into structural overspend with no recovery plan beyond statutory override
findings.detail: The DSG deficit for 2025/26 in-year is £24.524m. Added to the £17.566m carried forward from 2024/25, the cumulative deficit is now £42.089m. This is 'currently managed through a Statutory Override agreed nationally by government for DSG deficits through to March 2028.' The pressures are structural: £6.691m top-up funding to mainstream schools, £5.565m increases to special school funding from recent banding review, and £8.671m to independent providers. The council is investing in SEND hubs to manage demand but improvements are forecast to 'slow' the rate of increase, not reverse it. In 2028, the override expires and the authority will need to hold this deficit on its main budget.
findings.matters: A £42m cumulative deficit that is hidden from the main budget only until March 2028 is a future liability. When the override ends, this must be reflected in the authority's financial position or formally written off. It signals the costs of SEND provision are unsustainable within the national funding model.
findings.figures: 2025/26 in-year DSG deficit £24.524m; Cumulative DSG deficit £42.089m (£17.566m carried forward + £24.524m new); Statutory Override protection ends March 2028; Pressures: mainstream top-ups £6.691m, special school funding £5.565m, independent providers £8.671m
findings.quote: The overall 2025-26 outturn against centrally retained DSG is forecast to be £24.524m in deficit as at the end of December 2025... This figure is currently managed through a Statutory Override agreed nationally by government for DSG deficits through to March 2028.

findings.headline: Children's external residential placements overspend by £14.745m with demand continuing to grow despite investment in prevention, leaving no control point
findings.detail: Children & Young People is forecasting £12.109m overspend, of which £14.745m relates specifically to 'spend over budget forecast on External Residential Placements'. Of this, £11.470m is growth in spot/framework placements and £2.280m is high-cost Disabled Children's Team placements (5 new placements since January). The council notes it is 'striving to minimise' demand by investing in SEND hubs and mainstream school top-ups, but 'whilst spend on Independent Providers remains over budget, the rate of increase has slowed from a 64% increase during 2023/24 to a 31% increase during 2024/25 and a 27% forecast increase in 2025/26.' The costs are outpacing mitigation.
findings.matters: Residential placement costs for children are high-unit-cost, and once a child is placed, the cost locks in. Growth at 27% annually, even if slowing, is unsustainable. The council has run out of lever-pulls on prevention and is simply absorbing cost.
findings.figures: Children & Young People overspend £12.109m; External residential placements overspend £14.745m (including £11.470m from growth in spot placements, £2.280m Disabled Children's new placements); 27% forecast increase in independent provider placements for 2025/26
findings.quote: £14.745m spend over budget forecast on External Residential Placements. £11.470m is an increase in External Residential Spot/Framework placements... £2.280m relates to the Disabled Children's Team residential expenditure budget where we have had 5 new high-cost placements since January 2025.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £16.791m driven by uncontrollable demand and complexity increase, with cases transferring from health creating permanent cost base increase
findings.detail: Care & Wellbeing is projecting £16.791m overspend. The core issue is £18.605m of 'spend over budget purchasing' in Adult Social Care operations, of which £13.073m relates to supported living and block purchasing increases driven by 'an increase in complexity of care and provider market challenges around capacity and uplifts'. A further £5.550m pressure is due to 'nursing due to complexity and Continuing Healthcare cases transferred from health to local authority'. The council is trying to mitigate with £12.415m additional income from client contributions and health joint-funded packages, but this is not enough to offset base cost increases.
findings.matters: These are not one-off pressures but structural: increasing complexity, health service transfers, and provider market capacity constraints are permanent features. The council cannot 'save' its way out of this; every year the base cost for Adult Social Care will likely increase, making overall budget balance progressively harder.
findings.figures: Care & Wellbeing overspend £16.791m; Purchasing pressures £18.605m; SPOT residential increase £8.303m; Nursing increase £5.550m; ISF domiciliary increase £4.109m; Supported living block increase £13.073m
findings.quote: £5.550m increase in nursing due to complexity and Continuing Healthcare cases transferred from health to local authority... £13.073m increase in spend over budget on supported living and supported living Individual Service Funds due to an increase in complexity of care and provider market challenges around capacity and uplifts

findings.headline: Savings delivery at only 30% of target with £37.147m of brought-forward savings from 2024/25 explicitly deemed unachievable without structural transformation
findings.detail: The council targeted £59.876m of savings for 2025/26. Delivery is tracked at only 18.177m (30%) as at 31 December. Critically, £37.147m relates to savings brought forward from 2024/25 that were supposed to be delivered on an ongoing basis from this year onwards. The report states these brought-forward savings are 'now considered unachievable within the remainder of the financial year'. New savings identified for 2025/26 are only £4.483m delivered of £7.721m (58%), described as 'the easier to achieve savings have all been taken'.
findings.matters: A council that cannot deliver savings in successive years is in structural deficit. The failure to deliver £37.147m of carry-forward savings signals transformation is not landing. This means the overspend is not cyclical but reflects inability to operate within available resources.
findings.figures: Savings target £59.876m; Forecast delivery £18.177m (30%); Brought-forward 2024/25 savings £41.166m with only £5.804m delivered (14%); Unachieved savings 'tracker reds' £43.485m as at 31 Dec
findings.quote: The outcome of these two factors is that delivery of the brought forward savings is now considered unachievable within the remainder of the financial year.

findings.headline: Projected £50.745m revenue overspend after releasing reserves, with general fund balance moving from £34.280m surplus to £16.465m deficit without government emergency support
findings.detail: The council's General Fund Balance was budgeted at £34.280m for year-end. The Q3 position shows a projected overspend of £50.745m (after releasing £2.516m from the Financial Strategy Reserve), which would leave the authority with a £16.465m negative balance. This would be an illegal financial position. The council is entirely dependent on Exceptional Financial Support to retain even a £5m buffer.
findings.matters: A council unable to maintain positive reserves and dependent on discretionary government bailout presents extreme lending risk. The projected year-end position of £5m reserves on a £288.586m budget (1.7%) is far below prudent levels and leaves no resilience against any unforeseen variance.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance: £34.280m budgeted → £50.745m overspend → £16.465m deficit projected; Exceptional Financial Support requested £71.4m; potential year-end balance £5.001m
findings.quote: An initial General Fund Balance of £34.280m indicates that the projected variance would not be accommodated... The GFB would be exhausted and if projections are borne out, and the authority would be in an illegal financial position.

findings.headline: Business rates collection fund deficit of £2.557m attributed to increase in reliefs awarded
findings.detail: The £2.557m business rates collection fund deficit is attributed to an increase in the number of reliefs awarded. Business rate reliefs reduce taxable rateable values and are typically granted to struggling enterprises, signaling local economic distress.
findings.matters: A lender assesses local economic health and revenue base resilience. Growing reliefs indicate business sector weakness and eroding non-domestic rate income—a key revenue source for councils.
findings.figures: £2.557m business rates deficit; in-year deficit £2.526m driven by relief increases
findings.quote: The forecast deficit on the Non-Domestic Rates Collection Fund is attributable to an increase in the number of reliefs awarded.

findings.headline: Council tax collection fund deficit driven by £2.555m increase in bad debt provision
findings.detail: The council tax collection fund deficit is primarily driven by a £2.555m increase in the bad debt provision, indicating growing difficulty collecting council tax from residents. This signals both revenue risk and underlying financial distress in the council's area.
findings.matters: Rising bad debt is a leading indicator of collection risk and resident financial hardship. A lender views deteriorating collection performance as a threat to future revenue stability.
findings.figures: £2.555m increase in bad debt provision; in-year council tax deficit £0.647m
findings.quote: The estimated deficit on the Council Tax Collection Fund is due to an increase in the contribution to the bad debt provision.

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficit of £2.446m to absorb into 2026/27 budget amid financial emergency
findings.detail: Shropshire faces a combined Collection Fund deficit of £2.446m (council tax £1.206m, business rates £1.240m) that must be incorporated into the 2026/27 budget. This arrives as the council manages a financial emergency declared on 10 September 2025, requiring 'significant management action...to ensure the Council's financial survival.'
findings.matters: A lender evaluates cash position and budget headroom. A £2.446m reduction in available resources during declared financial crisis directly affects the council's ability to service debt and maintain operations.
findings.figures: £2.446m total deficit; £1.206m council tax; £1.240m business rates
findings.quote: Shropshire Council's share of the overall estimated deficit of £2.446m, comprised of an estimated deficit of £1.206m for Council Tax and an estimated deficit of £1.240m for NDR.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revised Auditors Annual Report - Shropshire Council - Final
findings.headline: LGA Peer Review July 2025 raised 10 recommendations including budget-setting process status
findings.detail: The LGA Peer Review highlighted the council's 'precarious financial position' and raised 10 recommendations. Notably, the review raised 'serious concern' that the budget-setting process had not commenced at the time of their visit, indicating organisational chaos amid financial crisis.
findings.matters: Independent peer review by LGA adding external validation of financial distress, and noting process failures suggests the council is not functioning normally in managing its finances.
findings.figures: 10 recommendations from LGA Peer Review; review conducted July 2025
findings.quote: The LGA Peer Review has recommended that the Council "prepare a clear whole council transformation plan that carries the aspirations and narrative for the future council and accurately aligns the resources for delivery. Ensure this is realistic widely understood and shared".

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revised Auditors Annual Report - Shropshire Council - Final
findings.headline: North West Relief Road project paused with significant unresolved funding gap; cancellation would require repayment of government funding to already-stressed reserves.
findings.detail: Work on the NWRR was paused in June 2025 following meeting with Department for Transport over a significant funding gap. A decision to cancel the project would require the council to repay government funding received, creating additional financial pressure on an already-depleted reserve position.
findings.matters: A forced repayment of substantial capital funding on an already-negative reserve position would likely trigger the Section 114 notice immediately, and represents a contingent liability creating additional downside risk.
findings.figures: Funding gap on NWRR significant enough to pause project; repayment amount not specified but acknowledged as material risk
findings.quote: the financial risk remains within the context of the Council's weakened financial resilience

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revised Auditors Annual Report - Shropshire Council - Final
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support of £26.9 million is temporary and increasing, with no sustainable plan to reach financial independence.
findings.detail: The council drew down £26.9 million of Exceptional Financial Support in 2024/25 to fund transformation costs and is seeking additional EFS for 2025/26. The audit emphasises EFS is temporary in nature and that repayment obligations and debt servicing costs will worsen future positions unless structural deficit is closed.
findings.matters: EFS is a stop-gap measure; mounting reliance on temporary support without a credible plan to return to sustainable finances indicates deepening structural problems and increased default risk.
findings.figures: £26.9 million EFS drawn in 2024/25; additional amount under discussion with MHCLG for 2025/26
findings.quote: EFS should be temporary in nature and the Council needs to clearly articulate the plan for reaching a financially sustainable position without undue reliance on temporary sources of support, which increase the debt profile of the Council and the associated ongoing revenue costs of servicing this borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revised Auditors Annual Report - Shropshire Council - Final
findings.headline: Council issued statutory recommendation by external auditors requiring immediate action on financial emergency, minimum viable service review, budget realism, and EFS exit plan.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton exercised statutory powers under the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 to issue a formal statutory recommendation requiring the council to: undertake immediate review of minimum viable service provision, eliminate optimism bias from budget assumptions, develop realistic plan to reduce reliance on Exceptional Financial Support, and implement Internal Audit budget monitoring recommendations.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations are formal enforcement tools; their issuance signals audit considers the council's arrangements so deficient as to require legal intervention, and non-compliance can trigger government action.
findings.figures: One statutory recommendation plus three key recommendations issued; council must consider at public meeting within one month
findings.quote: We have concluded that it is appropriate for us to use our powers to make written recommendations under Section 24 of the Act, due to the significant weaknesses we have identified in this report in relation to the current financial position of the Council and the forecast outturn position for 2025/26 potentially putting the Council into an unlawful financial position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revised Auditors Annual Report - Shropshire Council - Final
findings.headline: Adult Social Care outturn deteriorated £15m between month 11 and month 12 reporting in 2024/25
findings.detail: Internal audit review identified failures including incorrect application of financial assumptions, lack of communication between finance and Adult Social Care, missed opportunities to identify overspend earlier, and lack of reporting on actuals. These failures meant an unexpected £15 million deterioration went undetected until year end.
findings.matters: Large month-11 to month-12 movements indicate the council cannot reliably forecast its own outturn, undermining confidence in any current financial projections and demonstrating control weaknesses affecting financial resilience.
findings.figures: £15 million undetected deterioration in Adult Social Care outturn in final month
findings.quote: incorrect application of financial assumptions and monitoring, lack of clear communication between finance and Adult Social Care, missed opportunities to identify overspend earlier and lack of reporting on actuals that would have identified this issue

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revised Auditors Annual Report - Shropshire Council - Final
findings.headline: Internal audit has rated the council's internal control environment as 'Limited Assurance' for six consecutive years with no improvement and acknowledged lack of urgency in addressing findings.
findings.detail: For the sixth consecutive financial year, the Head of Policy and Governance (Internal Audit) issued a 'Limited Assurance' opinion. Internal audit has indicated there has been little improvement during 2025/26 and no evidence the council is addressing root causes of control failures identified in prior years.
findings.matters: Six years of limited assurance indicates systemic governance and control failures. The audit report explicitly links this to the council's current financial failures, including the Adult Social Care overspend crisis.
findings.figures: Six consecutive years of 'Limited Assurance' opinion (at minimum 2019/20 through 2024/25)
findings.quote: For the last 6 financial years the opinion of the Head of Policy and Governance (Internal Audit) on the internal control environment of Shropshire Council has been "Limited Assurance". There has been little, if any, evidence of the Council improving this situation and seeking to address the findings of the Head of Policy and Governance (Internal Audit).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revised Auditors Annual Report - Shropshire Council - Final
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reached £17.6 million in 2024/25 and is forecast to hit £36.9 million by March 2026, with statutory override expiring in 2028.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit increased by £15.096 million during 2024/25 to £17.639 million. The forecast for 2025/26 is an additional £19.323 million increase, taking the cumulative deficit to £36.888 million by March 2026. The statutory override mechanism protecting councils from this deficit runs only until 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: If the statutory override is not extended beyond 2028, the council will be liable for the full £36+ million deficit from its General Fund, which would be catastrophic given current reserve levels are already forecast to be negative.
findings.figures: DSG deficit at 31 March 2025: £17.639m (increase of £15.096m); forecast 2025/26 increase: £19.323m; cumulative at March 2026: £36.888m
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit held by Shropshire Council at 31 March 2025 was £17.639 million, an increase of £15.096 million from the opening position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revised Auditors Annual Report - Shropshire Council - Final
findings.headline: Council delivered £47.194m of £90.006m savings target in 2024/25 (52%); 2025/26 tracking £33.981m of £59.876m target (57%) with £25.894m at significant risk
findings.detail: The council's 2024/25 budget depended on £90.006 million in savings but only delivered £47.194 million (52%). For 2025/26 the requirement is £59.876 million but at period 5 only £33.981 million (57%) is expected, leaving £25.894 million (43.2%) at significant risk of non-delivery.
findings.matters: Repeated failure to deliver savings targets forces reliance on reserves or exceptional funding, undermining the credibility of any financial recovery plan and requiring validation of any savings assumptions in future forecasts.
findings.quote: The 2024/25 budget was dependent upon the delivery of £90.006 million of savings in year. The Council delivered 52% of this target, equating to £47.914m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revised Auditors Annual Report - Shropshire Council - Final
findings.headline: Medium-term financial gap has nearly doubled to £81.7 million for 2026/27, with cumulative £138.6 million gap to 2030/31.
findings.detail: The updated Medium Term Financial Strategy published in October 2025 shows the 2026/27 gap has increased from £36.193 million (February 2025) to £81.677 million. The cumulative gap across the full MTFS period to 2030/31 is £138.556 million with no clear plan to bridge this sustainably.
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this scale indicates the council cannot balance its budget without sustained exceptional support or radical service restructuring, making financial sustainability highly questionable.
findings.quote: This has now increased to a forecast gap of £81.677 million in the October 2025 update. The cumulative gap to 2030/31 is reported as £138.556 million. There is no clear plan on bridging this gap in a sustainable manner.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Revised Auditors Annual Report - Shropshire Council - Final
findings.headline: Shropshire Council faces imminent risk of Section 114 notice due to forecast £47 million overspend in 2025/26 against £34 million reserves.
findings.detail: The council delivered a £34.2 million overspend in 2024/25. The forecast for 2025/26 deteriorated significantly from £35.5 million (period 5) to £47.1 million (period 6) following detailed review of actual spend. With General Fund reserves of only £34.28 million, this would exhaust reserves entirely and potentially place the council in an unlawful financial position requiring a Section 114 notice.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration that a council cannot meet its spending commitments and triggers government intervention, severely restricting the council's financial independence and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £34.2m overspend 2024/25; £47.069m forecast overspend 2025/26; £34.280m General Fund reserves; forecast deficit £12.789m
findings.quote: At period 6 this position has deteriorated further to a forecast outturn overspend of £47.069 million. Delivering an overspend of this level would leave the Council with a negative General Fund reserves balance, potentially placing the Council in an unlawful financial position.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care budgets face structural uncontrolled demand pressure; 2025/26 budgets already need adjustment for 2026/27
findings.detail: ASC 'budgets were under pressure throughout the year, largely due to increasing demand and increasing complexity of service user needs.' The 2025/26 budgets were set before the outturn problem was known, so they too require adjustment for the 2026/27 setting process.
findings.matters: Structural demand in adult social care combined with insufficient grant funding drives recurring budget overruns. The council is chasing a moving target and its base budgets are not sustainable.
findings.figures: Increasing demand was the offset factor to in-year savings delivery; 2025/26 budgets require adjustment before 2026/27 setting
findings.quote: Within the People Directorate, Adult Social Care budgets were under pressure throughout the year, largely due to increasing demand and increasing complexity of service user needs.

findings.headline: Shropshire declared a financial emergency on 10 September 2025 and used reserves to cover the Adult Social Care deficit
findings.detail: The £31.2m overspend was offset using reserves. The council is now in financial emergency, implementing 'significant management action' to reduce spend for survival, including stopping non-essential spend and extending service delivery timescales.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown to cover operating deficits signals distress. A council in financial emergency has no capacity for additional borrowing and cannot fund discretionary capital or service development.
findings.figures: £31.2m deficit covered from reserves; financial emergency declared 10 September 2025
findings.quote: Shropshire Council continues to manage unprecedented financial demands and a financial emergency was declared by Cabinet on 10 September 2025.

findings.headline: Root cause: council did not track actual expenditure during the year, only forecasts, hiding the true position until year-end
findings.detail: Monthly monitoring used spreadsheets outside the ERP system. Actuals were not recorded during the year, preventing comparison of forecast to reality. Budget holders and Finance thought savings were on track based on their own data, but the ERP system producing official reports was never updated, masking the problem until reconciliation.
findings.matters: A council that cannot identify a £15m problem for 12 months has no effective financial control. This is not a forecasting error; it is a broken monitoring process that prevented the council from taking corrective action.
findings.figures: Issue not identified until year-end reconciliation; gap of 11 months between period 11 and final outturn
findings.quote: This reporting focused on the movement between periods and actuals were not recorded until the end of the year. The absence of actuals throughout the year prevented the opportunity to assess the robustness of forecasts and significant variances between forecasts and actuals throughout the year.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend jumped £15m in one month due to £11.7m of claimed savings that proved uncashable
findings.detail: Period 11 forecast a £16.1m People Directorate overspend. At period 12, year-end reconciliation revealed £31.2m, with £15m of that jump in ASC. The Internal Audit found that £11.7m of projected savings were not actually deliverable—the council believed it was achieving savings that were never real.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on a council's financial position when £11.7m of claimed savings evaporate at year-end. This shows fundamental inability to accurately forecast its own budget and raises questions about all forward projections.
findings.figures: £16.1m forecast period 11 vs £31.2m actual period 12; £15m ASC movement; £11.7m uncashable savings
findings.quote: at period 11, the People Directorate was forecasting an overspend at outturn of £16.1m, However, at period 12, following year-end reconciliation of expenditure, income and savings, this variance increased to a total of £31.2m, of which £15m of this movement was within ASC budgets.

news_drafts.headline: Shropshire's draft 2027-2032 plan says 2026/27 budget needed £121m of exceptional financial support
news_drafts.lead:
Shropshire Council could not have set a balanced budget for 2026/27 without exceptional financial support from government, according to its draft Medium Term Financial Plan for 2027 to 2032, which went to Cabinet on 18 November. Exceptional financial support is permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending. The plan puts the sum approved in principle for 2026/27 at £121m, against £71m for 2025/26.

The plan says that without the support the council's chief finance officer would have had to issue a section 114 notice, the formal declaration that a council cannot balance its budget. In its words: "Ultimately, without this EFS, the Council would have been unable to set a balanced budget for the year and it would have been necessary for the s151 Officer to issue a s114 notice."

The paper says the support was essential to restabilise the budget. It filled structural deficits in adults' and children's social care and removed unachievable savings targets from the base budget. The plan also says there is an ongoing risk of government intervention, including the appointment of envoys or commissioners, if the council cannot show a credible strategy to reduce its reliance on the support.

news_drafts.headline: Shropshire Council receiving exceptional financial support, with government monitoring and outside reviews
news_drafts.lead:
Shropshire Council is receiving exceptional financial support (EFS) from government, according to papers for its Audit and Governance Committee on 25 September 2026. EFS is permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort for councils.

The report describes the council as "receiving Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from the Government". It says the support comes under formal arrangements: the council must submit responses to external assurance reviews, which are reviews of its finances carried out from outside the council, and accept government monitoring.

The paper gives no figure for the support, so the amount is not stated in the material put to the committee.

news_drafts.headline: Shropshire pension fund faces significant cyber oversight gap, auditors warn
news_drafts.lead: An audit of Shropshire's pension fund has identified a gap in cyber security oversight rated "Significant" by the auditors—the only finding at that top priority level among 17 recommendations. The Internal Audit report found that the pension fund and the council's Information and Communications Technology (ICT) team do not hold regular meetings to oversee cyber threats, system changes, and incident management. The auditors recommended that "regular meetings [be] held between the Pension Fund and Shropshire ICT to ensure adequate oversight of cyber threats and risks." The finding was flagged as highest priority because the pension fund systems hold pensioner data and process benefit payments. Six audit recommendations on pensions administration procedures—including outdated policy logs and insufficient payroll controls—were rated as requiring attention.
